Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women remain a contender in deeper Pac-12 Conference | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
Editor’s note: This is the fifth and final story in a series examining the offseason for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program.

It’s not anywhere close to the original, but for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program the refashioned Pac-12 Conference that it will now call home will present plenty of challenges.

More so than the West Coast Conference – although the Zags’ final season in the WCC was arguably their most entertaining and tightly contested ever.

The WCC has historically been light on competitive depth. Last season was an outlier. Most years two, maybe three teams challenged for league and conference tournament championships.

The respect Gonzaga forged in the WCC will likely follow it into the Pac-12. In way-too-early 2027 NCAA Tournament bracketology, the Zags are picked to earn the automatic bid from the Pac-12.

The Zags are seeded anywhere from No. 7 to No. 10 in early 2027 NCAA Tournament brackets.

Of the nine Pac-12 teams, Gonzaga (24-10), Colorado State (27-8), Oregon State (23-12) and San Diego State (27-6) are expected to jockey for spots in the top four. But Washington State (9-25) and Boise State (25-9) will definitely have a say in how things play out.

San Diego State won the Mountain West regular-season title last year and Colorado State won the conference tournament to earn a bid to the NCAA Tournament.

“The level of play is going to be high and it’s going to be a very competitive conference season,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said.

Fresno State (15-18), Utah State (6-24) and Texas State (11-19) will likely finish in the lower third. Utah State tied for last in the Mountain West last season, and Fresno State and Texas State have new coaches.

“We’re going to get to play each other twice which is not all that common anymore,” Fortier said. “The Power 4 (conferences) don’t do that. And we didn’t do that in the WCC last year. We’ll get a true (regular-season) champion. I’m looking forward to that. We’re going to be pushed every night.”

The conference tournament format will be just like the WCC with the top two seeds receiving double byes to the semifinals and the No. 3 and No. 4 teams getting byes to the quarterfinals.

Of the new teams, Gonzaga is most familiar with Colorado State. The Zags lost in overtime two years ago in Ft. Collins, Colorado, and fell 70-66 at McCarthey Athletic Center last year.

“They’re tough every year,” Fortier said. “They’ve always been a contender to win the Mountain West.”

San Diego State returns four starters and Oregon State returns three from last year and a fourth who started two years ago is back after sitting out following knee surgery.

Washington State returns all of its starters and a sixth who started 20 games.

Based on the final NET rankings from 2025-26, the new fangled Pac-12 will be much stronger than the WCC.

Here were the final NET rankings for the teams that will comprise the Pac-12: Gonzaga (62), SDSU (66), Colorado State (67), OSU (85), Boise State (120), Fresno State (173), WSU (227), Texas State (251).

Here were the final NET rankings for the remaining WCC teams: Santa Clara (80), Loyola Marymount (108), Pepperdine (132), Portland (134), San Francisco (157), Saint Mary’s (183), Pacific (208), San Diego (268) and Seattle U (342). Denver (293) joins the WCC this fall.

Transfer portal, eligibility, recruiting

Gonzaga has had to use the transfer portal to fill roster holes the last two years. But Fortier hopes it will be a supplemental part of recruiting moving forward.

While many programs across the nation are leaning heavily into the transfer portal to sustain or improve, Fortier wants to resist the temptation. Gonzaga has been built on signing high school players and developing them. She doesn’t plan to deter from the formula.

“We’re pretty excited that we can finally do some building,” Fortier said. “It’s really challenging nowadays where you’re just reorganizing and trying to figure out who you have and what they can do with the way the transfer portal has been. It’s been so discombobulated.”

Fortier doesn’t have to harken back too far to recall the most recent team she developed largely through high school signings. The 2023-24 team, which posted the best record in school history (32-4), started five seniors, four in a fifth year who had signed with Gonzaga out of high school. Whether that can happen again remains to be seen.

The recent change in eligibility rules means it could be at least another two years before Gonzaga dips deep into the high school pool.

The new age-based eligibility the NCAA adopted beginning in 2026-27 allows athletes five years of eligibility to be completed within a strict five-year period. Returning players are grandfathered into the new rule and receive an additional year of eligibility unless they’ve already used a redshirt or medical waiver.

Fortier said 11 of 12 players on her roster are eligible for an additional year. The exception is sophomore Lauren Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and medical waiver.

The Zags have four seniors on the 2026-27 roster – Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso, McKynnlie Dalan and incoming transfer Jocelyn Medina. Fortier said she will determine which players want to return for another season at a later date.

Gonzaga has an oral commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Alyah Cornwall for the 2027 recruiting class. At this point Cornwall is the lone commitment for the early signing period in November.

The 5-foot-8 Cornwall is a true point guard – pass first, score second. It’s been a few years since the Zags had a point guard with a quarterback mindset.

Still, Cornwall can score. In 28 games last year at G-Prep, she averaged 17.9 points, 9.9 rebounds, 5.3 assists and 3.3 steals. She was the Greater Spokane League most valuable player and defensive player of the year.

“She loves getting other people involved,” Bullpups coach Geoff Arte said. “But she can really score it too and finishes around the rim. She loves to push the basketball and get it up ahead.”

Fortier said she’s not certain if she’ll sign others. NCAA rules allow schools to have 15 athletes on scholarship. With 12 players Fortier has some options.

Nonconference

Gonzaga will have fewer conference games than it has had in the WCC with just nine teams in the Pac-12.

Additionally, the NCAA expanded the number of games schools can play from 31 to 32. With 16 conference games that means Gonzaga has scheduled 16 nonconference contests.

Gonzaga is finalizing many of its nonconference games including a tournament in Hawaii where the Zags will take on Cal on Nov. 23.

What is known is Gonzaga opens the season at home Nov. 2 against North Dakota State, a return game from a year ago when the Zags opened at NDSU. Nov. 2 is the earliest date any colleges can play this season.

Another announced opponent is Michigan State in a neutral court matchup with the Gonzaga and Michigan State men Dec. 19 in Palm Springs, California.

The Zags will complete a two-year agreement with Arizona State, traveling to Tempe, Arizona, on Dec. 6.

A familiar nonconference opponent returns to the schedule with Montana, which visits Gonzaga Nov. 18. It’ll be an interesting matchup considering the Grizzlies picked up former Gonzaga guard Paige Lofing in the transfer portal this spring.

Those are the known dates at this time. Gonzaga will travel to Stanford and also will play Eastern Washington.

Gonzaga will also have return games at home against UC Riverside and at Grand Canyon.

“I think it’s really going to be a tough (nonconference) schedule,” Fortier said. “We have a couple of really hard games. But I think this team is up for it.”

Another Fortier milestone

Fortier tied LSU coach Kim Mulkey as the fastest coach to reach 300 career victories last season.

Looking back, Fortier said reaching 300 wins didn’t mean much to her.

“I’m just happy for the players and for the (assistant) coaches,” Fortier said. “We care more about how many weddings we get to go to and which babies we get to hold and which players come back. We like to watch them be successful in their life (after basketball).”

Whether she likes it or not, Fortier is closing on another milestone and it’ll happen quickly in the 2026-27 season. Going into her 13th season with her faithful assistants who include her husband Craig, Stacy Clinesmith and Jordan Green – each of whom have been around as long as she has – Lisa Fortier will become Gonzaga’s all-time winningest coach.

She has a 313-84 record (.788 winning percentage). She’s four wins from passing Kelly Graves, who she succeeded. Graves was 316-186 (.699) in 14 seasons.

“I would just say that I’m just grateful to have been part of the building of the program and get us to that place where we were able to just continue and take it to the next level,” Fortier said. “And now I’m ready for us to hopefully take what we’ve done to the next level as well.”

Gonzaga.title: 'Man, it's going to pass.' New Gonzaga wing Chauncey Wiggins navigated summer of uncertainty before earning fifth year
Gonzaga.summary:
Chauncey Wiggins gave Florida State’s upset bid a jolt of life with 37 seconds left during an ACC Tournament quarterfinal game against top-ranked Duke last March.

With the Seminoles trailing 80-77, Wiggins received the ball on the right corner and went to work on Duke’s Cameron Boozer, backing the Naismith Award winner down until he got to his spot outside of the paint. That’s when Wiggins used his long frame to pull up over the sturdy, 6-foot-10 center, and sink a 13-foot step back shot that trimmed the Blue Devils’ lead to one.

The clutch jumper represented the 967th and 968th points of Wiggins’ career – the last ones he’d score as a college basketball player. Or so he thought.

Florida State came out on the wrong end against Duke, losing 80-79, and subsequently turned down an invitation to play in the NIT, signaling the end of Wiggins’ college journey.

The wing was prepared to turn the page, fulfilled with how his four college seasons played out. He made consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances at Clemson, playing key bench minutes for the 2023-24 team that advanced to the Elite Eight. Under first-year Florida State coach Luke Loucks, he averaged double figures for a group that claimed the Seminoles’ first winning ACC record since 2020-21. He nearly eclipsed the 1,000-point milestone, posted a career win-loss record of 92-45 and earned academic honors at Clemson in 2024.

An All-ACC selection would’ve been a nice bonus, but outside of that Wiggins didn’t have too many complaints with his college resume.

“I thought college was over,” Wiggins said. “I thought it was a good four years. Making it to March Madness, that was my dream. I wish I’d gotten on the All-ACC team but I didn’t. I thought my college career was done.”

As Wiggins went through the pre-NBA draft process, there were murmurs that he and other class of 2022 high school graduates might have another shot to play college ball through the NCAA’s new age-based eligibility rules, permitting student-athletes to play five seasons over five years.

Wiggins didn’t think much of it as he traveled for NBA workouts with the Miami Heat, Los Angeles Lakers, Phoenix Suns, Sacramento Kings and Dallas Mavericks, eventually latching on with the Boston Celtics for NBA Summer League in Las Vegas.

“I literally kept telling one of my friends, ‘This thing ain’t going to happen at all, we’re not getting another year,’” Wiggins said. “Then a few weeks after that, our class didn’t get grandfathered in. So we were like, yeah it’s done.”

One friend, former Utah State guard MJ Collins Jr., was insistent, telling Wiggins, “Man, it’s going to pass.”

Not long after he completed his Summer League assignment with the Celtics, Wiggins returned home to Atlanta and began to monitor the college basketball news cycle, eventually learning Collins Jr., new Gonzaga point guard Javon Bennett – a transfer from Dayton – and other players in Ohio had challenged the NCAA in court to secure another year of eligibility.

Wiggins got together with family members, his agent and a lawyer to explore the possibilities, eventually joining a separate group of fifth-year hopefuls seeking a similar injunction in his home state of Georgia.

After finishing a workout on July 31, Wiggins opened up social media and learned about the class-wide injunction in Colorado that granted fifth-year seniors in all sports an extra year of eligibility. Less than a week later, a state judge ruled in favor of Wiggins and other players who filed in Georgia, giving the transfer wing another layer of security.

“So I’m kind of double-protected, if that makes sense,” Wiggins said.

Before either ruling, Wiggins was already hearing from high-major college programs around the country, including Gonzaga, Georgia, SMU, Washington and the Florida State program he recently played for. Wiggins also had pro options on the table, including a G League offer from the Kings and an opportunity with a club team in Japan’s top league.

At Gonzaga, his point of contact was assistant coach RJay Barsh, who worked on Leonard Hamilton’s staff at Florida State in 2022-23. Wiggins and Barsh didn’t overlap in Tallahassee, but the Gonzaga assistant was familiar with the wing’s game from Florida State’s encounters with Clemson in the ACC. It also helped they had a mutual friend in FSU assistant Director of basketball operations Ryan Shnider, a former graduate assistant under Hamilton who stayed on staff when the Seminoles hired Loucks.

“From a basketball standpoint, (Barsh) was recruiting me just saying you’re going to play 2, 3, 4 here,” said Wiggins, who primarily played the 4 and occasionally as small-ball 5 at his last two schools. “Even when he said the 2, I was kind of surprised. … He was like, we’ve got some good length and good guys here. He said we have positions but just say if you get the rebound, you’re going to push the ball and now you have to know what to call. Then obviously coaches can say that and not mean it. Obviously I’m an older guy so I know what I want. Also I had to ask him, can I see some clips of this?”

Shnider also had a relationship with Jalen Warley, who successfully made a similar transition from Florida State to Gonzaga, where he was one of Mark Few’s most valuable two-way players during last year’s 31-win campaign. Wiggins reached out to Warley to get an honest and transparent evaluation of Gonzaga’s program, coaching staff and culture.

“He really loved it there,” Wiggins said. “He really loved it, had a lot to say about the coaches in a positive way. I was like, hey just be realistic. He was like the coaches, what they say is true basically.”

An Atlanta native who’s only resided in Georgia, South Carolina and Florida, Wiggins was familiar with Gonzaga but couldn’t have identified Spokane on a map of Washington. (He admits he originally thought it was a suburb of Seattle). By the time he was born in 2004, the Zags had already planted their flag on the national stage, and Wiggins became accustomed to hearing the school’s name every year, usually whenever March rolled around.

“I watched Gonzaga when I got into college and when I was in high school, but even when I was a kid I always heard of some school called Gonzaga,” Wiggins said. “They always make it to March Madness, they always win, they’re always putting people in the pros, they have a good coach.”

A 13.3 point-per-game scorer last season at Florida State who made 38.7% of his 3-pointers, Wiggins is encouraged by all the possibilities at Gonzaga. The 6-10 wing has seen and enjoyed the online discourse about potential lineups featuring him next to 6-7 Davis Fogle, 6-11 Braden Huff and 7-1 Massamba Diop.

“That was really (Barsh’s) pitch and saying, with your shooting ability, we’re adding your shooting ability so that’s really going to open up things for everybody on the floor, whether that’s your shooting or B-Huff’s hook shot or Diop, with them doubling the center,” Wiggins said. “It’s just going to open up a lot. Coach Few’s system, a lot of movement, not really standing in the corner. It was a really good pitch and obviously it got me here.”

Wiggins plans to spend the next few weeks working out back home in Atlanta with a longtime personal trainer, “Coach BB” of SmallBall Training, and shooting coach Bobby Perez before moving to Spokane ahead of fall practices.

On the surface, outside shooting projects to be the most valuable asset Wiggins will bring to a Gonzaga program that posted the lowest 3-point percentage of Few’s 27-year tenure last season (34.0%). Wiggins wants to keep that aspect of his offensive game sharp, but the veteran wing is also looking to improve his ball-handling and defense.

“I’m really showing people I can be even more versatile, really just working on putting the ball on the floor more,” Wiggins said. “Rebounding more, crashing offense, defense. I’m always still working on my defense. Offense, just putting the ball on the floor, making sure the shooting is staying sharp, post game if I ever need to and touch around the basket.”

Gonzaga.title: Former Gonzaga star Brandon Clarke's death ruled accidental overdose of cocaine, heroin
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Gonzaga forward Brandon Clarke died of an accidental overdose of heroin and cocaine, the L.A. County Medical Examiner ruled in a report released Friday.

The medical examiner also listed the “combined effects of multiple prescription medications” as a significant contributing factor in his death. A full autopsy report will be released at a later date and will include the names of those prescriptions, the medical examiner’s office said.

Clarke, a beloved teammate who spent his entire NBA career with the Memphis Grizzlies, died May 11 at a residence in Southern California. The 29-year-old former Gonzaga standout was found unresponsive in his bedroom, according to the coroner’s report.

Following his death, the Grizzlies said in a statement that they were “heartbroken by the tragic loss.” Clarke had struggled with injuries during the past three seasons, but when healthy he was one of the most impactful bench players in the NBA.

“Brandon was an outstanding teammate and an even better person whose impact on the organization and the greater Memphis community will not be forgotten,” the team wrote.

Clarke played 309 games over seven seasons for Memphis, with the team reaching the playoffs four times. The Grizzlies said Clarke was expected to make a full recovery ahead of next season. He had a year remaining on his four-year contract worth $12.5 million annually.

Clarke was pronounced dead after the Los Angeles Fire Department responded to an emergency call at a residence in the 20300 block of Del Campo Place in Woodland Hills at just after 5 p.m. May 11. Paramedics pronounced him dead at 5:15 p.m.

His death came six weeks after he was charged in Arkansas with felony counts of trafficking of a controlled substance and fleeing law enforcement at speeds topping 100 mph. Deputies alleged that he had 235 grams of kratom, a controversial plant-based substance that is not approved by the Food and Drug Administration, in a duffel bag in his car at the time of his arrest April 1.

While kratom is considered a felony narcotic in Arkansas, it was legal in Tennessee, where Clarke owned a home, at the time of his arrest. The coroner’s report did not note the presence of kratom.

Clarke was also facing misdemeanor counts of drug possession for a THC vape pen he was carrying and for making unsafe lane changes and speeding. He was scheduled to appear at an arraignment May 15 at the St. Francis County District Court in Forrest City, Arkansas. Following his death, the case was dismissed.

Clarke was born in Vancouver, Canada, and raised in Phoenix. He was part of a Gonzaga team with Los Angeles Clippers forward Rui Hachimura that was one of the greatest in school history. Clarke is remembered not only for his NCAA Division I-leading 68.7 field-goal percentage, but for his warm and kind spirit.

He was drafted in the first round of the 2019 NBA draft.

“He was just so easy to coach,” Gonzaga head coach Mark Few said. “Every time you’d see him walking around the facility, he had a smile on his face.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga makes second 5-in-5 addition with commitment from Florida State wing Chauncey Wiggins
Gonzaga.summary:
Chauncey Wiggins scored a victory in state court on Wednesday morning, securing another year of eligibility through a preliminary injunction that featured more than a dozen other players in his home state of Georgia.

By Thursday evening, the talented Florida State transfer who played two seasons at Clemson and recently appeared at NBA Summer League for the Boston Celtics had another reason to celebrate, announcing a commitment to Mark Few and Gonzaga.

Agent Daniel Hazan of Hazan Sports confirmed the wing’s commitment to On3.com’s Joe Tipton, giving Gonzaga its second “5-in-5” transfer in as many days.

Dayton point guard Javon Bennett, an All-Atlantic 10 First Team selection last season, committed to the Zags on Wednesday after being deemed eligible through a similar lawsuit in Ohio.

Dozens of players in three separate state lawsuits – Ohio, Tennessee and most recently Georgia – have taken the NCAA to court, pursuing another year of eligibility through the governing body’s new age-based eligibility rules, giving athletes five years to play five seasons.

Although the NCAA stated it wouldn’t approve a blanket waiver to include last year’s senior class, Wiggins, Bennett and others have been successful challenging the organization in state court, earning injunctions that, for the time being, should enable both to compete for Gonzaga in 2026-27.

Uncertain if another college season was in the cards, Wiggins went through the NBA draft process and joined the Celtics at Summer League in Las Vegas, where he averaged 3 points and 2 rebounds while averaging 7.7 minutes over three games.

Wiggins is able to return to college basketball because he joined the Celtics’ roster through a Summer League invite and didn’t sign an NBA two-way or Exhibit 10 contact.

While Bennett helped the Zags address one of their holes in the backcourt, Wiggins provides something different as a 6-foot-10 wing who averaged 13.3 points and 3.9 rebounds last season as a 30-game starter at Florida State.

Both players should help address outside shooting deficiencies for a program that posted the two worst 3-point percentages of Few’s tenure in successive seasons.

Bennett made 90 3’s last season at Dayton, connecting at a clip of 34.7% on seven attempts per game. Wiggins took 5.8 3’s per game at Florida State, but was one of the most efficient shooters in the ACC, making 38.7% of his attempts.

Before Florida State, Wiggins played a total of 97 games over three seasons at Clemson, appearing in 27 games as a reserve as a freshman before starting in 18 of 36 games as a sophomore and transforming into a primary starter as a junior, making 26 starts in 34 appearances. Wiggins averaged 8.3 ppg and 2.9 rpg as a junior, shooting 43.8% from the field and 36.5% as a sophomore.

The Atlanta native played on a Florida State tam that missed the postseason after finishing 18-15 overall and 10-8 in the ACC under first-year coach Luke Loucks, but he made five NCAA Tournament appearances at Clemson, getting reserve minutes in each of the Tigers’ four games during a 2024 run to the Elite Eight. Wiggins was also on Clemson’s NCAA Tournament team in 2025, scoring 10 points in an opening-round loss to McNeese State.

An experienced wing who’s played in 129 career games, Wiggins should figure into Gonzaga’s rotation and will have a chance to compete for starting minutes in the frontcourt alongside transfer center Massamba Diop (Arizona State) and returning forward Braden Huff.

Wiggins was able to move to his third school because he entered the transfer portal in the spring, months before his case was heard by a judge in state court. Upon entering, the Florida State wing was ranked by 247Sports as the 65th best overall player in the portal.

“He found the perfect style of play (at Florida State) where his size and shooting from 3 in a spaced-out and offensive system can shine,” 247Sports.com’s Travis Branham wrote earlier this week in an analysis of Wiggins. “… He isn’t a physical presence down low, but anyone in need of floor spacing will be highly interested in adding the four-star transfer.”

Wiggins’ announcement elicited a reaction on Thursday from Jalen Warley, another wing who had college stops at both Florida State and Gonzaga and spent two seasons facing the 6-foot-10 forward in the ACC.

“Great move!!” Warley wrote, commenting on an Instagram post announcing Wiggins’ commitment.

With Wiggins, the Zags have 12 players either signed or committed to the 2026-27 roster. Wiggins, Bennett and international prospects Nathan De Sousa and Izan Almansa have all committed to GU but have yet to ink financial aid agreements.

Gonzaga.title: Bremerton's Jalen Davis names Gonzaga among 10 college finalists
Gonzaga.summary:
Days after scheduling an official visit to Gonzaga, four-star combo guard Jalen Davis named Mark Few’s program as one of his 10 finalists.

The top-rated prospect from Washington in the recruiting class of 2027 will also consider Stanford, UCLA, Ole Miss, BYU, Washington, Iowa, Texas Tech, USC and TCU, he told Joe Tipton of On3.com Thursday morning.

A standout at Bremerton High, where he plays under his father Jeremiah, Davis recently told 247Sports.com’s Brandon Jenkins he’s planning to visit Gonzaga for the team’s home opener on Nov. 7 against New Mexico State.

Davis is scheduled to visit four of his other finalists – Iowa, UCLA, Stanford and Ole Miss – before closing out his fall recruiting tour with a cross-state trip to Spokane in early November.

A 6-foot-3, 165-pound combo guard known for his shot-making, Davis is rated as the top overall player in Washington and the third-best player at his position by 247Sports. The recruiting service also considers him the nation’s No. 17 overall prospect.

“Davis is a skilled guard who differentiates himself with his feel for the game, processing ability, and understanding of how to be a high-volume scorer without having to dominate the basketball,” 247Sports recruiting director Adam Finkelstein wrote of Davis. “He put up more than 23 points per game in the 3SSB season on better than 49% shooting from the floor while playing largely off the ball. He moves without the ball extremely well. He’s a good cutter, knows how to use screens, and is still a highly effective passer.

“There aren’t many players in high school basketball who can read a pindown and then make a pocket pass if the big helps on his catch, but Davis is one of them. His ability to make quick reads and decisions is one of the most impressive parts of his game.”

A Gatorade Player of the Year in Washington, Davis led Bremerton to its second straight Class 2A championship in March while averaging 31.5 points, 9.6 rebounds, 5.8 steals and 5.2 assists. He shot 63.9% from the field and 40% from the 3-point line as a junior, leading the Knights to an overall record of 26-2.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with depth, experience, Gonzaga women can focus on little things: 'Possibilities ... are vast.'
Gonzaga.summary:
Editor’s note: This is the fourth story in a multipart series examining the offseason for the Gonzaga women’s basketball program.

The Gonzaga women’s basketball team is two months away from measuring how much offseason individual improvement has taken place.

GU coach Lisa Fortier anticipates a much more cohesive and versatile team than a year ago.

“We have the pieces in each position group that we put out there,” Fortier said. “We just have to figure out how we take them to the next level, how do we take our team shooting to the next level, how do we take our team rebounding to the next level and how do we learn to guard better as a group.”

Going into the 2025-26 season, the Zags had many unanswered questions. It started with experience – mostly experience in a Gonzaga uniform. The Bulldogs returned one starter.

There should be a marked difference in 2026-27. The Zags return four starters and five others who saw consistent time off the bench. The nine players will account for most of the playing time with two transfers and a freshman as the lone newcomers.

“We’re not freshmen to college, we’re not freshmen to workouts, we’re not freshmen to practice and pressure and those things,” Fortier said.

Gonzaga is coming off a 24-10 season that ended with an 81-66 loss to Ole Miss in an NCAA Tournament opener. The Zags hope to use how they finished in that game as a springboard into bigger and better things this year.

“We should have some confidence that we’re a good team,” Fortier said. “There are a lot of people who made big impacts that are back. I would hope that they want to keep chasing improvement, knowing what the possibilities are for this team. There’s a lot of possibilities for what this team can do.”

It’s not getting too far ahead to talk about where Fortier wants to see this team specifically and the program in general go.

“We can be a pretty good team … the possibilities for this team are vast,” she said. “Things we’ve never done before are attainable with this group. We’re just working to stay true to the process. We’ve got to work on how we show up for every individual workout and how we show up for every weight (conditioning) session. The little things done well will add up to big things.”

The Zags finished as the No. 1-ranked team in the nation in 3-point made percentage (39.2), just ahead of UConn.

Gonzaga should increase that percentage this season with capable long-distance threats. Junior-to-be guard Allie Turner led at 47.1% (89 of 189), followed by junior guard Teryn Gardner (46%, 52 of 113). Sophomore forward Lauren Whittaker made 35.5% (33 of 93) but wants to make significant improvement this season. Others are expected to shoot effectively from long range as well.

The Zags’ versatile offense will assist in shooting percentages, to be sure. When defenses are forced to account for the 6-foot-3 Whittaker, 6-2 sophomore forward Jaiden Haile and 6-2 senior forward Taylor Smith will give perimeter players plenty of open looks.

Another forward, 6-foot graduate transfer Sierra Lichtie, who was slowed by injuries last year, had a season of eligibility left but decided to move on after finishing work on a master’s degree, Fortier said.

Gonzaga outrebounded opponents by 10 per game last year. That, too, is an area Fortier expects improvement.

The Zags also will emphasize upgrades defensively. They allowed opponents 65 points per game last year, and opponents shot 40% from the field.

Position-by-position defense will be key, but Fortier said the Zags are better when they defend as a team. Better defense means the offense can play freely and doesn’t have to outscore opponents to cover for defensive liabilities.

“We need to embrace some team defensive things,” Fortier said. “How do we learn how to guard as a group, guard better individually but also find a way to help each other and cover for each other a little more? That’s an area we struggled with at different times last year.”

By and large, though, the Zags have few questions to answer going into the season. The roles of the two transfers and lone incoming freshman will be among first order of business when preseason practice begins.

The 2026-27 roster includes the fewest first-year Zags since 2023-24, when Gonzaga added two freshmen and no transfers.

Gonzaga had to use the transfer portal the last two years to replenish a roster hit by graduation and transfers. The Zags brought in four transfers two years ago and four more last season.

Turner was the lone freshman added two years ago and Haile, Julia Wilson and now-departed Paige Lofing made up last season’s freshman class.

The newest additions this season are 6-1 freshman forward Abby Lusk of Pocatello, Idaho; 6-foot junior wing/small forward Emmy Roach, a transfer from Rider; and 5-6 senior guard Jocelyn Medina, a transfer from Denver.

With a deep returning roster, it’s unlikely any of the newcomers will challenge for a starting position. But they will definitely be in the mix for valuable minutes off the bench.

Of the three newbies, Lusk may have an opportunity to make the biggest impact. Out of necessity, she had to play point guard for her high school team last year, leading Pocatello to a state championship.

“She’s perfect for us,” Fortier said. “She’s versatile. She plays with great pace. She wants to get better. She can handle the basketball. She has all the tools. It’s always an adjustment to go from high school to college, but if you don’t have the tools in high school then it’s even harder to build them in college. She’s starting off with the appropriate skill set. We did not miss on the type of kid we got with Abby.”

Washington State.title: WSU hosts FCS Duquesne, looking to bounce back from two straight losses to open year | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home opener against Duquesne on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

In new head coach Kirby Moore’s home debut, WSU is set to host FCS Duquesne, which is coming off two straight losses to open the season. The Cougars are doing the same, so with an opportunity to kick-start an offense that ranks last nationally in total offense, this game might have a little extra meaning for the hosts.

Outside of WSU’s long-running series with nearby Idaho, it’s the Cougars’ first time hosting an FCS opponent since earning a 70-30 win over Portland State in 2024.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 12:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

USA Network will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around a 35.5-point favorite in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

In a 34-7 loss to Kansas State, dropping WSU to 0-2 for the first time since 2016, the Cougars’ offense fell flat. That group did not score, the first time the program has gone scoreless on offense since 2010, and quarterback Caden Pinnick completed just 9 of 20 passes for 65 yards, becoming the first WSU QB to pass for fewer than 100 yards since Jeff Tuel did it in the same season, back when Paul Wulff was head coach.

WSU scored once, a pick-six going into halftime from safety Jaylen Thomas, who picked off two passes total in the game. But the Cougars didn’t score otherwise, totaling just 166 yards of offense, giving them 408 yards of total offense and 204 per game – both of which rank last in the country. Running backs Kirby Vorhees and Maxwell Woods combined for just 74 yards, and Vorhees lost a fumble for the second straight game.

It was also another sluggish outing from WSU’s special teams department. In the first quarter, kicker Jack Stevens sent a field -goal attempt too low, allowing it to get tipped at the line of scrimmage, giving him three misses in his first four tries to open the season. And in the second quarter, the Cougs permitted a 62-yard punt return, giving the Wildcats a chance to score a touchdown two plays later to secure a 17-0 lead.

The visitors’ defense was hardly perfect – one of the biggest problems was that WSU generated just seven pressures on K-State QB Avery Johnson – but their offense was the main culprit behind this loss. The Cougars were playing without top wide receiver Tony Freeman, who is now expected to miss the rest of the season due to a torn ACL, taking away a key component of his team’s offense and kick/punt return game.

“Well, I think you go back. Have had a lot of meetings, really getting off the flight, and then yesterday in the morning,” Moore said. “Starts back with our process of game planning, the number of reps we get in practice, how many looks we get of those during the week. Obviously, that’s gonna build confidence for the players and what could come on Saturday. Everyone being on the same page – that’s the one thing about offensive football. Gotta have all 11 working together. At the end of the day, we gotta score more points to be successful here.”

WSU also didn’t have either of its starting cornerbacks, Jalil Tucker (out with injury) and Khamari Terrell (out for undisclosed reasons). Each are expected to be available in Saturday’s game against Duquesne, Moore said.

Scouting Duquesne …

The Dukes are coming off two straight road FBS losses to open the season, a 34-0 defeat to Air Force and a 70-13 setback at the hands of Youngstown State. They rank last in the FCS in total offense, posting just 351 total yards, and they’ve also lost a pair of turnovers .

Duquesne is led by head coach Jerry Schmitt, who is in his 22nd season at the helm of the program. He’s taken the Dukes to the FCS playoffs three times in his tenure, most recently in 2023.

This year, the team’s quarterback is sixth-year journeyman Carson Camp, who started his career with three seasons at South Dakota before spending the 2023 and 2024 seasons at Sacramento State. He transferred to Southeastern Louisiana, where he threw for nearly 1,800 yards before moving over to Duquesne . In two games this fall, he has completed just 12 of 37 passes (32%) for 105 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions.

The Dukes also rank seven spots up from last in the FCS ranks in total defense, allowing an average of 526.5 yards per game.

“Offensively, they do a good job with RPOs and got an experienced quarterback. He’s entering his seventh year in college football,” Moore said. “Very solid running backs. No. 32 (Ness Davis) was an all-conference player last year, and defensively they have seven new starters, so a little bit of a new group there.”

What happened last time?

This will be the teams’ first-ever meeting.

Washington State.title: 'I need to be a better image': WSU QB Caden Pinnick addresses short postgame message after loss to Kansas State
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Shortly after Washington State wrapped up its last game, a blowout road loss to Kansas State over the weekend to drop coach Kirby Moore’s team to 0-2 to open the season, Cougar quarterback Caden Pinnick was short on words.

On some of the team’s biggest problems on offense, Pinnick said only, “We just lost. Next question.”

On what was holding back WSU’s passing offense, which produced only 65 yards, Pinnick said, “Good team. We lost.”

On whether he felt like offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s playcalls were putting the team in the best positions to succeed, Pinnick said, “It’s not for me to say. We just gotta get better.”

On Monday, Pinnick led off his news conference addressing that postgame session, which lasted less than two minutes, saying it was “not quite the response that you want.”

“As you lose two games in a row, emotions can be high,” Pinnick said, “and as a quarterback of this team and university, it is my job to give this team and institution some pride and belief. My frustrations from the past two weeks crept up on me, got the best of me. It was a growing process for me as well, and looking to get better.”

Pinnick, who completed just 9 of 20 passes for 65 yards in Saturday’s game, is the face of a WSU offense that is still finding its footing. After two games, the Cougars rank last in the country in both total offense (408 yards) and points per game (8.5). Against K-State, Pinnick became the first WSU QB to pass for fewer than 100 yards since Jeff Tuel did so in 2010, which was also the last time a WSU offense went scoreless in one game.

The Cougs have also played a grueling two games to open the season, facing road contests against Power 4 foes Washington and Kansas State. That raises this question: How many of the Cougars’ problems are products of the opponents they’ve played, and how many are issues they could correct on their own?

“Honestly, a lot of them are on me,” said Pinnick, a redshirt sophomore transfer from FCS UC Davis. “Whether it’s getting guys lined up in correct formation and proper verbalization in the huddle. But credit to the teams that we played. I’m a realist, and I’ve spoke to the team and just kinda put it in perspective: we’ve played two really good defenses that have been established.

“This is a new offense, yes, and we’re all starting to learn and get familiarized with it. I don’t think there’s anything negative to take away, other than, yeah, let’s move the ball some more. Let’s simplify some things, and let’s just be better.”

Pinnick, 20, is under a spotlight he has never been before. He acknowledged that on Monday, saying that he’s had to lean on several kinds of people to make this adjustment: His mother, Heidi, plus his coaches. He also admitted these kinds of settings aren’t as common at UC Davis, saying, “That’s something that I’m continuing to grow in, coming from a smaller place. You don’t get a lot of that, and so this is a daily growing process.”

“I think after a really bad offensive performance for two weeks straight, I think your mind is all over the place,” Pinnick added. “You just come to your senses 24 hours after an incident. You realize like, yeah, I was wrong. I need to be a better image for my team and my guys. Acknowledging, like, hey, yeah, we lost, but what’s gonna change? That just clicked to me, and it helped me realize that, as someone who’s my position, I gotta act better.”

Even outside of Saturday’s postgame incident, Pinnick and the WSU offense are under scrutiny. The Cougars failed to record an offensive touchdown last weekend, putting offensive coordinator Matt Miller under the microscope. It’s forced Moore, a longtime friend and former teammate of Miller at Boise State, to answer some questions.

That includes this question: Is the idea that Moore should take over some playcalling duties an overreaction?

“Well, I think everything’s up for evaluation,” Moore said. “I think the most important thing is we gotta work together. And like I said, we’re having a lot of meetings, looking at our process, looking at our practice plans, looking at how many reps we get, how many calls are on the call sheet. All those things need to be looked at because we gotta put our guys in the best position to be successful.”

For WSU, that’s the other side of the calculus. Are Miller and his playcalls delivering on that idea, putting the Cougs in the best positions on offense?

“Collectively, we gotta play better,” Moore said. “Whether it’s the in-the-week process, whether it’s carrying that over to Saturday and trusting everything that we’ve done during the week, that’s gonna be the big focus, and I wanna help with that.”

Washington State.title: WSU WR Tony Freeman to miss rest of season with torn ACL, plus other injury updates
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State wide receiver Tony Freeman has played his final snap of the season.

Freeman is expected to miss the rest of the season with a torn ACL, coach Kirby Moore said Monday, dealing a costly blow to the Cougars’ receiving and kick return departments. A senior and a team captain, the speedy Freeman was expected to be his team’s top option on both fronts.

Freeman’s injury happened during WSU’s season-opening loss to rival Washington on Sept. 6. Freeman played just 10 snaps before going down with his injury, going to the locker room and returning in street clothes.

WSU’s medical staff is still determining Freeman’s surgery date, Moore said, adding that it’s possible Freeman returns for an extra season next fall. But that much is unclear at this point.

A year ago, Freeman started seven of 13 games, reeling in 54 passes for 590 yards and three touchdowns. In the punt return department, he also recorded an average punt return of 17.3 yards, the sixth-best mark nationwide and a WSU single-season record. He also set a program record with 415 punt return yards on the season.

Freeman’s absence figures to be another tough development for WSU’s offense, which ranks last nationally in total offense (408 yards) and points per game (8.5). In the Cougars’ loss to Kansas State on Saturday, their offense went scoreless for the first time since a a blowout loss to Arizona State in 2010, when Paul Wulff was head coach.

That’s a key reason behind the Cougars’ 0-2 start to the season, the program’s first since 2016. On Saturday, quarterback Caden Pinnick passed for just 65 yards, becoming the first WSU signal-caller since Jeff Tuel registered fewer than 100 passing yards in 2010.

A quick slot receiver, Freeman’s absence figures to push other WSU receivers into the spotlight. In Saturday’s game, Cougar wideouts Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons combined for just 41 yards on five catches. Transfer receiver Tank Hawkins, who started the game but played only one snap, could wind up in a bigger role as well.

WSU could also ask a bit more from veteran receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy, who caught one pass for 11 yards against K-State. That was the Cougs’ first third-down conversion of the season.

“Darrius made a couple plays there. BG’s stepped in,” Moore said. “We gotta find ways to get them the ball. D-Blood first game, I think, didn’t get as many there in the second game. And then Jordan Dees and Tank Hawkins gotta find roles and find opportunities as we progress here.”

Other injury updates

In other injury news, WSU starting cornerbacks Khamari Terrell and Jalil Tucker are expected to be available for Saturday’s game against FCS Duquesne, Moore said. Terrell didn’t travel to Kansas State due to a concussion he suffered during practice last week, Moore said, while Tucker traveled but watched from the sideline in street clothes.

Those two absences cost the Cougars’ defense, which surrendered 487 total yards to the Wildcats, including 192 passing from quarterback Avery Johnson and another 295 rushing. WSU’s replacements on defense were Kai Rapolla and Jamarey Smith, the latter of whom moved from nickel to cornerback. Rapolla allowed four catches on five targets, according to Pro Football Focus, while Smith permitted just one catch on five targets.

It was a bit of a slow game for Rapolla, who finished with an overall PFF defense grade of just 52.2, so Terrell and Tucker’s returns should boost WSU’s defense. Tucker got hurt in the Apple Cup, when he went airborne to break up a tipped pass and a UW defender tackled him at the knees.

• WSU defensive ends Michael Hughes and Malachi Wrice are expected to miss Saturday’s game nursing their own injuries, Moore said. Hughes, who didn’t play against K-State, is expected to miss a couple weeks with a leg injury, while Wrice is considered week-to-week.

Both Hughes and Wrice are backups, but their absences could loom large for WSU, who has two stars at that position in Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk. But now the Cougars’ depth will be tested. It’s possible the Cougs ask more from defensive ends like Ben Beatty and Fernanco Lecuona (20 snaps apiece against K-State), plus Arizona transfer Eduwa Okundaye, who played 11 snaps in Manhattan.

“All those guys, we gotta rotate and be fresh up front,” Moore said, “and that’s gonna be important.”

Thomas named Pac-12 Defensive Player of the WeekIn Saturday’s game, Jaylen Thomas delivered two interceptions, including a 50-yard pick-six going into halftime. That helped him earn Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Week honors, according to a Monday release.

He’s the first WSU player with multiple interceptions in a game since Sam Lockett III had two against Arizona in November 2022. He’s also the first Cougar defender to record multiple interceptions with at least one returned for touchdown since Armani Marsh in the 2021 Apple Cup.

Thomas also became the first WSU player to post a pick-six since former linebacker Taariq Al-Uqdah did so in 2024 against Oregon State.

“I love Jaylen Thomas, just working with him on a daily basis,” Moore said. Obviously, coach (Greg) Burns had experience with him in the past (at San Jose State). He’s a student of the game. He works his tail off. He’s up on the fifth floor multiple hours outside of the players’ hours, meeting with coach Burns, talking with coach (Trent) Bray, and I think that’s shown up on the field.”

Washington State.title: Cougars Fall to Kansas State 34-7
WSU safety Jaylen Thomas' two-interception day highlights otherwise sluggish outing from Cougar defense in loss to Kansas State
Washington State.summary:
MANHATTAN, Kan. – Jaylen Thomas felt something stir in him, like his Washington State team needed someone to make a key play. The Cougars were looking at a two-score deficit late in Saturday’s game, and as the clock ticked under 10 seconds in the second quarter, the Wildcats were looking to add on.

So Thomas followed through on what his brain was telling him. He watched K-State quarterback Avery Johnson’s eyes, watched him load up and target a receiver near Thomas’ area. So when Johnson let it go, Thomas leapt in front, snagging an interception and taking off the other way, outrunning everyone to the end zone.

With that, Thomas recorded a 50-yard pick six, handing the Cougars a jolt of momentum headed into the intermission. That was his second interception of the game, the first coming earlier in the second quarter. It helped Thomas finish with by far the best outing among Cougar defenders in this one, earning a Pro Football Focus coverage grade of 91.0, which will likely hold as one of the best coverage marks in the country for this week.

“We needed to make a play on defense,” Thomas said, “and I ended up doing my job, which led to an opportunity, and I made the best of that opportunity, as you guys saw. The one thing I was really happy about was the first thing I seen was my teammate P3 (Paul Hutson III) running down the field, going to block for me. So that just made me really excited, really encouraged for the type of camaraderie we have on our defense, on our team as a whole.

“I felt like that switched the whole momentum of the game,” Thomas added of his pick-six, the first by a Cougar defender since Ethan O’Connor did it in 2024. “We were going into halftime hype, we were up. But I would just say that was a very positive play for our team, and I’m glad that I was a part of it.”

All told, Thomas totaled two interceptions and four tackles – all of the solo variety. He was just about everywhere on defense. That didn’t do much to slow the Wildcats’ offense, which produced 34 points as Johnson passed for 192 yards and three touchdowns, but there’s no denying that Thomas did his part.

If Thomas’ production comes as a surprise, check out what he did during the Cougars’ fall camp. He piled up three interceptions in team periods, including two on Pinnick. That also includes one pick six. He’s a playmaker, so to speak, so the way he stepped up in Saturday’s game should not come as a complete and utter shock.

Here’s the ironic part: Thomas didn’t actually start Saturday’s game. He was on the bench to begin the game behind Jackquintin Ball, who wound up playing 20 snaps. But before long, Thomas, who made his coaches look wise, replaced Ball.

Overall, though, WSU’s defense will have to be a bit better moving forward. It’s important to note that the Cougars played this game without starting cornerback Jalil Tucker, who head coach Kirby Moore said was out with “a little nick.” Tucker is expected to be available for WSU’s next game, Moore said, a home matchup with FCS Duquesne next weekend in Pullman.

WSU produced just seven pressures on K-State QB Avery Johnson, according to PFF, with only two coming from defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk – the two edge rushers the Cougars needed to make a big splash in order to pull this upset. That didn’t happen, which goes a long way in explaining how Johnson broke free for 192 yards passing and another 78 rushing.

“All around, we gotta be better,” said WSU defensive tackle Kaden Beatty, who picked up two tackles, one for loss. “Again, I gotta watch the tape. I don’t know exactly where the holes were, the breakdowns, but 34 points? That’s not our standard. We wanna hold donuts on people, and that’s what we’re gonna do. So we need to get back, watch the tape, and there’s no losses. It’s only lessons. We’re gonna grow from this, and we’re gonna be better.”

Washington State.title: After going scoreless in blowout loss to Kansas State, WSU's offense has real questions to answer | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
MANHATTAN, Kan. – After the blowout had finally come to an end, after Washington State’s offense wrapped up a scoreless day in a lopsided loss to Kansas State here on Saturday afternoon, Cougar quarterback Caden Pinnick didn’t have much to say.

What were some of the main problems on offense?

“We just lost,” Pinnick said. “Next question.”

What was holding back WSU’s passing offense, which produced just 65 yards?

“Good team,” Pinnick said. “We lost.”

Do you feel like OC Matt Miller’s playcalls are putting your offense in the best positions to succeed?

“It’s not for me to say,” Pinnick said. “We just gotta get better.”

Whatever you think of his approach in this scenario, Pinnick didn’t provide many answers for the way WSU’s offense languished in this 34-7 loss, dropping the Cougars to 0-2 for the first time since 2016. For the game, Pinnick completed just 9 of 20 passes for 65 yards, becoming the first WSU signal-caller to pass for fewer than 100 yards in one game since Jeff Tuel did so in 2010. The Cougars’ scoreless offensive showing is also the program’s first since 2010, when Paul Wulff was head coach.

Needless to say, that’s not company WSU coach Kirby Moore wants to keep. Even in the program’s most listless offensive outings, like a blowout loss to Arizona in 2023 or a shocking road loss to Cal in 2017, the Cougars managed to put up points on offense. That wasn’t the case here in Manhattan, where WSU couldn’t even find a way to punch in a garbage-time touchdown, which the Cougs did even in a road rout against North Texas last season.

There’s also this problem: In Saturday’s game, the WSU offense converted just 2 of 12 third downs. Add that to the Cougars’ effort in last weekend’s Apple Cup, when they went 0-for-11, and they have started the season with a 2-for-23 conversion rate on third down. That’s barely 9%, which requires rounding up.

We could sit here all day and write superlatives about this WSU offensive game, but you get the point already. The Cougs looked bad. Overstating just how bad might be a challenge. What’s more interesting is how many of this unit’s problems are because of the circumstances – facing a Big 12 team on the road on a short week, going up against a talent disparity, being without top receiver Tony Freeman – and how many could the Cougars conceivably turn around?

“Still first and second down. You go back to that,” Moore said after the game, referencing the biggest problems with his team’s offensive effort. “I don’t know the exact third-and-long and XL numbers, but I think that was fairly high again. We gotta create explosives in those situations. Trying to put together eight, 10, 12-play drives versus a defense like K-State, that’s gonna be pretty difficult.”

Moore had a point about his team’s problems generating chunks of yards on first and second down. The Cougars’ average yards-to-go on third down was 9, which is unsustainable against just about any opponent, much less a Power Four one like the Wildcats.

But here’s the thing: WSU faced exactly the same problem in last week’s Apple Cup against Washington, which is the reason this feels discouraging for the Cougars. They didn’t make any meaningful adjustments.

Headed into this game at K-State, much of WSU’s offensive success figured to hinge on the speed with which offensive coordinator Matt Miller could make adjustments. That cost WSU in the Apple Cup, when the Cougars found success rolling out of the pocket and running to the outside – but that took Miller three quarters to realize.

Against Kansas State, Miller didn’t appear to have learned his lesson. The most striking example came in the second quarter, when the Cougars were facing a third-and-2 from the Wildcats’ 37. Miller went with a middle run for running back Kirby Vorhees, who gained just 1 yard. It felt like the kind of play call a coordinator makes when he was already planning on going for it on fourth down, and at the plus-37, that’s a fine idea.

The problem was the play Miller went with next: a QB keeper up the middle for Pinnick, who was met immediately at the line of scrimmage, turned away for no gain and a turnover on downs.

That prompts what is beginning to feel like a pressing question: Is Miller’s play calling putting the Cougars in the best positions to succeed?

“We gotta look at that,” Moore said. “Naturally, I think just the third and fourth down – that was probably a big one there in the first half. They did a good job. They stopped us. You look at that sequence there of plays and kinda the numbers and what the defense did as well.”

Before we go further, we should detail this bit of context: WSU is in the midst of one of the most grueling opening schedules in the country, going on the road to face Washington and then Kansas State. The Cougars were expected to lose to UW by about 24 and K-State by about 19. These are not the kinds of opponents that the Cougars will face in Pac-12 play, which is when we can probably start judging this team in earnest, not against Power Four opponents at their houses. These two games are a tall task for just about any team in the country, not just Washington State.

Still, the Cougars’ play calling has left much to be desired, no matter the opponent in these first two games. On that front, in Saturday’s game, a few other sequences stood out like sore thumbs. After a weather delay, the Cougars got the ball to start the second half. They were riding a nice wave of momentum thanks to safety Jaylen Thomas’ pick-six to end the half. If they could put together a scoring drive here, they could pull within one score and make things interesting.

Instead, here is how WSU’s drive unfolded: False start on right guard Nick Bakken. Vorhees rush for 6 yards. Pinnick incompletion. Pinnick incompletion. It was a quick three-and-out for the Cougars. Their defense went on to surrender a long touchdown rush moments later, putting the Wildcats up 24-7.

“Just gotta execute,” Pinnick said when asked about that sequence.

Bakken’s false start provides a nice segue into the other part of this problem for WSU, which is its offensive line. The Cougars’ front five permitted two sacks, according to Pro Football Focus, with the third sack chalked up to other reasons. Left tackle Ashton Tripp, who gave up one of those to star edge rusher Wendell Gregory, finished with a PFF pass-blocking grade of just 1.9 – about as bad as it gets. Right tackle Jaylin Caldwell, who subbed in in the second half, registered a figure of 11.9. And left guard Kyle Martin, who was benched to start the second half before returning later in the game, finished with a mark of 30.7.

The numbers are a bit better in the run-blocking department. Bakken graded out really well, finishing at 85.5, which is far above average. Jonny Lester, who started at right tackle before moving inside and later getting benched when the game got out of hand, was at 74.4. Caldwell and Tripp each checked in around the mid-60s.

Perhaps what stands out most: Martin finished with a run-blocking grade of 49.4. Pair that with his pass-blocking grade, the aforementioned 30.7, and you start to see a problem. You go back to last week’s Apple Cup, when Martin earned a pass-blocking grade of 8.7 and a run-blocking grade of 38.1 – both lowest on the team – and the problem becomes even more serious. Could the Cougars reconfigure their offensive line, the way they did in the second half, when Martin went to the bench?

It’s important to note that those numbers could change, in either direction, as PFF amends their grades in the next day or two.

Whatever is going on along WSU’s offensive line, it’s not helping the Cougars’ offense, which got just 45 rushing yards from Vorhees and 29 from Maxwell Woods, the second straight game each has been held under the 50-yard mark. To their credit, WSU coaches mixed things up on the offensive line in Saturday’s second half.

Is that the culprit behind these two miserable outings from the Cougs’ offense? It’s entirely possible. What about the play from Pinnick? That’s also a real possibility. Next week, WSU hosts FCS Duquesne, which should be an easy win for the Cougars. It’s likely they’ll bounce back, and that could give them real momentum going into the following game, a home matchup with Arizona.

Still, WSU’s offensive outing here on Saturday won’t inspire much confidence. The Cougs’ offense, their play calling, will have to improve in big ways to change that.

Washington State.title: Washington State falls flat in all phases during blowout loss at Kansas State | Instant reactions
Washington State.summary:
Washington State’s offense had another troubling performance. And the defense wasn’t great either. Playing their second straight road game against a power-conference opponent, the Cougars struggled mightily during a flat Week 2 effort, falling 34-7 on Saturday against Kansas State at Bill Snyder Family Stadium in Manhattan, Kansas.

Offense causes more concern

The Cougs had no rhythm for three quarters last week during their Apple Cup loss. On Saturday, WSU’s offense looked considerably worse . The group failed to score, punted eight times, went three-and-out (or four-and-out) on six possessions, converted on 2 of 12 third downs and finished with a measly 166 total yards during one of their least productive offensive games in recent memory.

The play calling was often conservative. Openings weren’t there for deep passes. The ground game was thoroughly uninspiring, resulting mostly in small gains, or no gain at all. The Cougs only got into scoring position on one drive – their first – and that ended in a tipped short-range field goal that looked like it was going to miss no matter if Kansas State got a hand on it.

Quarterback Caden Pinnick had a miserable outing, completing 9 of 20 passes for just 65 yards. Misreads were prevalent, and receivers couldn’t separate downfield. WSU did end up surpassing 100 rushing yards, but much of that came in the later stages with K-State ahead comfortably. The Cougars too frequently ran into walls for minimal gains.

Clearly, offense is the most glaring issue for this WSU team.

Defense can’t hold forever

The bright spot in last week’s loss, WSU’s defense had a tough outing against the Wildcats, surrendering 487 yards and plenty of chunk plays – including five rushing plays of 15-plus yards, topped by a 75-yard K-State touchdown run through a wide-open gap early in the third quarter that deflated WSU’s hopes of a comeback.

It certainly didn’t help that WSU’s defense was constantly put in difficult positions by its offense. The defenders were on the field for long stretches as K-State’s offense plugged away downfield with several long drives. The Wildcats had possession for over 34 minutes. K-State’s time of possession in the first half doubled WSU’s. It’s hard to defend effectively without time to rest.

That said, WSU’s defense couldn’t come up with big stops, allowing K-State to convert on 8 of 10 third downs in the first half. When Wildcats quarterback Avery Johnson escaped pressure in the pocket, he found faults in WSU’s pass coverage – two of his three TD passes came on broken plays. And the Cougs just couldn’t get to Johnson in the backfield, failing to record a sack and managing four TFLs in the run game, allowing the Wildcats to pile up 295 rushing yards (7.4 yards per carry).

Cougars safety Jaylen Thomas tried to singlehandedly keep his team afloat in the first half, jumping out routes for two second-quarter interceptions. He returned his first pick, early in the second quarter, to the K-State 45-yard line, but the Cougars offense did nothing with it, immediately turning the ball over on downs with some head-scratching play calls – four consecutive runs up the middle.

Thomas’ second pick resulted in WSU’s only score. K-State quarterback Avery Johnson got greedy with seven seconds left in the first half, tossing an errant pass toward the sideline. Thomas was in perfect position, snatching a pick and racing 50 yards to the end zone to cut the deficit to 17-7.

After an hour-long weather delay during the half, it felt like WSU could come out of the break with momentum. Instead, the Cougars went three-and-out to open the third quarter, and the WSU defense was sent right back out. On the Wildcats’ first play from scrimmage, K-State running back Rodney Fields Jr. gashed the Cougs’ defense, darting through an open lane in the left side of the line and loping 75 yards for a touchdown, putting K-State up 24-7 and extinguishing any momentum WSU thought it had.

Rough start for new Cougs

Of course, it’s a less-than-desirable start for new coach Kirby Moore and Co. Two difficult road games against Power Four teams resulted in an expected 0-2 record. Week 1 had promising signs. Week 2, not so much.

But the Cougars should get a reprieve next week, when they host FCS Duquesne. Perhaps the team will get a much-needed confidence boost. Maybe it’ll give the Cougs and new offensive coordinator Matt Miller, who’s taken plenty of heat over the past two weeks, a chance to sort out some of their many issues offensively and find a flow.

Without trying to sound too optimistic, it’s important to remember that this WSU team is operating with a completely reworked roster and first-year staff. It takes time to build confidence and stability in new schemes. Having said that, it doesn’t inspire much confidence getting steamrolled by a K-State team that’s also playing under a first-year coach. The Cougars need to sort a lot out soon, because Arizona is coming to town in two weeks before the Pac-12 schedule begins.

Washington State.title: Defensive end Wendell Gregory helps Kansas State lock down Washington State offense | Difference makers
Washington State.summary:
KSU DE Wendell Gregory

The junior Oklahoma State transfer spearheaded a lock-down effort from Kansas State’s defense, which flustered Washington State all afternoon and held the Cougar offense scoreless. Gregory sacked WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick twice and had a tackle for loss in the ground game. Gregory sped past WSU right tackle Jonny Lester and brought Pinnick down on a third-down play in the second quarter, leading to a punt and a K-State scoring drive that put the Wildcats up 17-0. Gregory breezed past Ashton Tripp on the right side for another third-down sack early in the third quarter, forcing a punt that led to a K-State field goal that gave the hosts a 27-7 advantage. Gregory tied for the team lead with five tackles and had three of K-State’s eight tackles for loss, helping the Wildcats limit WSU’s offense to 166 total yards and just two third-down conversions.

WSU S Jaylen Thomas

The first-year Cougar snagged two interceptions and accounted for all of WSU’s scoring, returning a pick 50 yards for a touchdown as time expired in the first half. Thomas blanketed a K-State receiver on an out route, but Wildcats quarterback Avery Johnson tried to test the coverage anyway, and Thomas jumped the pass with ease, then had plenty of space to maneuver to the end zone. The defensive score cut the K-State lead to 17-7. Thomas, a San Jose State transfer, recorded his first career interception earlier in the second quarter, reading Johnson’s eyes and snatching an ill-advised fourth-and-8 throw on an out route near the left sideline, then returning that interception 31 yards to the K-State 45. WSU’s offense couldn’t do anything with it, though, quickly turning the ball over on downs. Thomas finished with four tackles.

Washington State.title: Despite pedigree, Washington State's offense hasn't shown much bite to start season | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
Caden Pinnick, who competed for and won the role of frontman and face of the Washington State offense, had this to say to a series of questions after failing to lead the unit to a single point on Saturday.

“We just lost. Next question. … Good team. We lost. Will get better. … Not for me to say, got to get better.”

Inspiring stuff.

Saturday’s 34-7 loss at Kansas State was hard, violent and frustrating. Unfortunately for the young Cougars quarterback, leadership is more about showing up and demonstrating accountability when everything hurts after a loss than it is reveling in the victories. You inspire more loyalty by taking ownership of shared failures than you do by doling out praise after individual triumphs.

Not that there has been much glory to share through two games in which the WSU offense has scored the same number of touchdowns as its defense: just one.

It has been a confusing start for the WSU offense. I don’t think I was alone in assuming that first-year head coach Kirby Moore would bring some offensive sizzle to Pullman. After all, the man has spent his life around offenses that cooked.

This is a guy who caught 131 passes for 2,126 yards by himself his senior year at Prosser High School, better numbers than many high school offenses put up all year. He played college ball on Chris Petersen’s legendary Boise State teams that will forever be remembered for creativity and inventiveness.

He cut his coaching chops at Fresno State under Kalen DeBoer and Ryan Grubb, who rode offensive excellence all the way to the national title game with Washington and then prestigious coaching jobs at Alabama.

And then, given the reigns as offensive coordinator at Missouri, Moore led an explosive offense that became one of the only few to ever produce a 3,000-yard passer, 1,500-yard rusher, and 1,000-yard receiver in the same season.

So why are we now watching this boring stuff? In a tough road game in which the Cougars trailed throughout, the coaches called mostly runs, many of them straight into the teeth of a defense that proved well-equipped to handle them.

The sad thing is the Cougars appear to be wasting a pretty good defense. One that has the size and depth to hold up against UW’s talented linemen in the Apple Cup, and the playmakers to seize on chances and create opportunities as with Jaylen Thomas’ pick-six to end the first half and give WSU life against Kansas State.

Something must change, and it can. Some of Mike Leach’s best seasons as WSU’s coach started with horrible losses and listless offenses. The 2016 team lost its first two games before reeling off eight straight wins. The year prior, the Cougars began with a terrible home loss to Portland State and ended the season beating Miami in the Sun Bowl.

Just last year, the Cougars’ offense had meager beginnings. Then coach Jimmy Rogers made the tough call to switch starting quarterbacks, a bold swing that paid off as the Cougars made it to a bowl game.

Two games in and this WSU team may be in need of a similarly bold swing. Without a proven backup such as Zevi Eckhaus to turn to, might I suggest Moore take the offensive play-calling reigns back?

Yes, head coach is a full-time job and it is usually preferred to hand off play-calling duties to the offensive coordinator. Certainly, many offensive-minded head coaches have held onto those duties for the sake of their ego for far too long.

But Moore cannot recognize the great offenses of his past in what the Cougars are running out of the huddle. Maybe it’s time for the head coach to show his quarterback how to take more ownership.
