Washington State.title: Why Kansas State will beat Washington State | The pick
Washington State.summary:
MANHATTAN, Kan. – In a realistic sense, headed into Saturday’s game at Kansas State, the deck is stacked against Washington State.

The Cougars are likely to be without top receiver and kick returner Tony Freeman, who is nursing a knee injury. They’re playing a game at what their body clocks will think is 9 a.m. And they’re doing it all on a short week after playing their season opener on Sunday.

For all those reasons and a few more, we’re taking K-State to handle WSU in Saturday’s game, which will be televised by TNT and streamed by HBO Max.

The Cougars’ offense played a key role in making things interesting in the fourth quarter of the Apple Cup, leading two scoring drives, but it was a forgettable outing all things considered. As his unit tries to improve on a three-turnover outing, WSU quarterback Caden Pinnick gets a K-State defense that may have some holes, but whose pass rush figures to be a challenge for a new-look WSU offensive line.

It’s reasonable to expect WSU offensive coordinator Matt Miller to be quicker to make adjustments in Saturday’s game – the time it took for him to do so in the Apple Cup was a key reason behind the Cougars’ offensive struggles in that game – but here’s predicting it won’t make a difference on Saturday. The talent gap between these two teams may not be as wide as the game’s 18.5-point spread may suggest, but it still exists.

In something of an understated storyline, special teams aren’t working in the favor of WSU, whose replacements for Freeman in the kick and punt return games couldn’t handle the ball in their opportunities. Contrast that against the Wildcats’ special teams units, which have produced 63 total return touchdowns since 2005 – tops in the FBS by a wide margin.

A loss wouldn’t be a complete indictment on the Cougars, who are working through a grueling opening stretch to their season. They’re expected to lose this game. It’s probably better to hold true judgment on this group until Pac-12 play arrives, but even so, they could be looking at their first 0-2 start since 2016.

Final score: K-State 23, WSU 10

Washington State.title: Washington State's keys to victory against Kansas State | 2-minute drill
Washington State.summary:
Washington State at Kansas State

Saturday, 9 a.m.(11 a.m. local time)Line: K-State favored by 17½

TV: TNT/HBO MaxRadio: 920-AM

Key matchupWSU edges vs K-State OL: Washington State’s edge rusher duo of Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk, who combined for nine quarterback pressures in last weekend’s Apple Cup, might be licking their chops. They’ll get a chance to match up with K-State left tackle Ryan Howard, who played his first career college game in a lopsided win last weekend, and right tackle Gus Hawkins, who played in seven games last season before going down with an injury. How that duo fares against McLain and Zunk will likely go a long way in determining how Saturday’s game unfolds. The Cougars played exceptionally well in the Apple Cup, but they didn’t produce a turnover, which they will likely have to do to pull an upset on the Wildcats. There’s lots of ways that could happen, but the likeliest formulas involve some combination of WSU’s defensive front, including linemen like Kaden Beatty, Paul Hutson III and Jirah Leaupepetele – the last of whom laid the foundation for WSU’s goal-line stop against UW.

If that group can generate significant pressure on Kansas State senior quarterback Avery Johnson and force a turnover, the visitors might have a chance. If not, things could get away from them.

How the Cougs win …

A potential WSU win would probably involve some combination of the Cougars’ defense creating multiple turnovers and their offense kicking into gear. Quarterback Caden Pinnick and that group helped make things interesting in the fourth quarter of last week’s game in Seattle, but overall, it was mostly a slog for the Cougs: Three turnovers, two missed field goals and a grisly 0-for-11 on third down.

If the Cougars want to earn a win this Saturday, they will have to improve in all those departments. Pinnick and WSU offensive coordinator Matt Miller can’t spend half the game trying something that isn’t working – last weekend it was running up the middle – and they have to be quicker to make adjustments on the fly. In the Apple Cup, Pinnick was at his best rolling out of the pocket, which could be the case again in Manhattan.

Complicating things for Washington State is the likely absence of top receiver Tony Freeman, who is nursing a knee injury he suffered in the first quarter of the Apple Cup. He also handles punt and kick return duties, which didn’t go well for the Cougars’ replacements, who mishandled one punt and one kickoff each.

How the Wildcats win …

Kansas State can earn this win by shutting down WSU’s offense, which gets another stiff challenge, especially along its offensive line. In the Apple Cup, the Cougars’ front five yielded one sack on 13 pressures, which isn’t a promising way to head into Saturday’s game, no matter how imposing the Huskies’ defense was. This time, the Cougs’ offensive line will have to hold off pass rushers like Wendell Gregory, Darien Whitaker and Jordan Allen, who combined for one sack and nine total pressures in an easy win over FCS Nicholls last weekend.

The spotlight will be on WSU’s tackles, Ashton Tripp and Johnny Lester, but the Cougars’ interior could be vulnerable as well. Left guard Kyle Martin finished with a Pro Football Focus pass-blocking grade of just 8.7 last week, which could make him a target. If he and his group can’t protect Pinnick and the Cougs’ offense struggles to get going, it could be a long day for WSU.

Key stat: 38

In last Sunday’s Apple Cup, WSU’s running back trio of Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi combined for just 38 rushing yards. Pinnick spearheaded his team’s ground attack with 61 rushing yards, but to swing an upset on Saturday, the Cougs will have to get more from a RB group that entered this season with sky-high expectations.

Biggest questionCan the WSU defense generate a turnover? For WSU, the clearest path to an upset involves a turnover or two from its defense, which could make things much easier on its offense. In terms of extenuating circumstances, the deck is stacked against the Cougars: The game will kick off at 9 a.m. on their body clocks, they’re on a short week and they’re headed into a second straight raucous environment.

To overcome those conditions, WSU needs its defense to come away with an interception or fumble recovery.

QuotableWSU tight end Jack Pedersen on the team’s short week: “It all just happens a little bit quicker. The 9 a.m. kick I don’t think will be an issue. I mean, we’re playing football, right? So you should be excited no matter what.”

Washington State.title: To pull an upset on Kansas State, WSU's offense will have to improve in a big way
Washington State.summary:
MANHATTAN, Kan. – Jack Pedersen likes to say he’s an early riser anyway. In his fifth and final season of college football, which he’s spending playing tight end for Washington State, he’s usually up and at ’em by 7 or 7:30 a.m.

With that approach, Pedersen gets a head start on his days, which mostly center around classes and practice in Pullman. He’s made the most of them, playing a shade over 50 snaps in WSU’s season opener, a loss to rival Washington in last week’s Apple Cup.

“We’re playing football. Why not be excited to go play?” Pedersen said. “Another great opportunity to play in a great atmosphere as well.”

But for Pedersen and the Cougars, this weekend’s game is a bit different. WSU players and coaches will have to be up even earlier than that to prepare for a road test against Kansas State, which is set for 9 a.m. on TNT and HBO Max. In the programs’ first meeting, the Wildcats are about 17.5-point favorites.

To avoid starting their season with two losses, the Cougs (0-1) won’t just have to wake up a bit earlier than usual. They’ll also have to play better than they did last week, in a 24-10 loss to Washington, which might start with their offense. In that one, WSU lost three turnovers, missed two field goals and didn’t score until the fourth quarter, which robbed coach Kirby Moore’s team of chances to climb back into the game.

For WSU, it’s another Power 4 game in a lineup full of them to kick off the season. The Cougars took a loss to the No. 17 Huskies last weekend. On Saturday, they have the Big 12’s Wildcats. Then on Sept. 26, they’ll host Arizona to complete their nonconference slate. Their path to earning bowl eligibility, which they’ve secured in 10 of the last 11 full seasons, becomes much easier with a win in Saturday’s game.

In perhaps the biggest news on that front, WSU will likely be without top receiver Tony Freeman, who went down with a knee injury just 10 snaps into last weekend’s Apple Cup. He’s also the team’s best punt and kick returner, and without him, the Cougars couldn’t field one punt and one kickoff cleanly. His absence looms large for Washington State.

Without Freeman, how can WSU QB Caden Pinnick and offensive coordinator Matt Miller facilitate a better outing? Against K-State (1-0), which opened its season with a 71-3 romp over FCS Nicholls last weekend, the Cougars will likely have to be quicker on the trigger to make adjustments. If they meet a similar fate as last week and can’t run up the middle against the Wildcats’ defense, which permitted just 102 yards against Nicholls, they’ll have to design more packages for Pinnick to roll out and for the Cougars’ running backs – Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi – to hit the outsides.

However WSU’s offense operates on Saturday, it’ll have to be better against a K-State defense that includes several key playmakers. Defensive end Wendell Gregory, a transfer from Oklahoma State, registered four quarterback pressures last weekend. Linebacker Darien Whitaker, who registered a strip sack, could also line up on the edge. Linebacker Mekhi Mason is questionable with an injury, but two other defenders could make an impact this weekend: Linebacker Gabe Powers and safety Logan Bartley each tallied five tackles against Nicholls.

Mostly, though, the Cougars will need to keep the pressure off Pinnick. That’s the responsibility of WSU’s offensive line, which gave up three sacks last week. This weekend, that group gets the challenge of blocking edge rushers like Gregory, Whitaker and Jordan Allen, who combined for one sack on nine QB pressures last week. Can WSU tackles Ashton Tripp and Jonny Lester keep them at bay? What about interior pieces like center Noah Dunham and left guard Kyle Martin, the latter of whom registered a PFF pass-blocking grade of just 8.7 last weekend.

“After every drive, just looking forward to the next and what can we fix? Where can we be better?” Pedersen said of his team’s offensive showing last weekend. “In my opinion, you don’t want to dive too deep into the iPads and everything. You just wanna go play and be free. What’s done is done in those plays. Let’s move on to the next drive and get better.”

If there’s any way the Cougars can pull the upset, it might start their edge rushing duo of Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk. Against Washington, they combined for nine quarterback pressures. They’ll have a similar opportunity against K-State, which suffered a setback before the season when John Pastore, a preseason all-Big 12 first team selection, went down with a season-ending injury. Junior Ryan Howard, who played his first snaps of college football last weekend, takes Pastore’s spot.

If WSU’s defensive front can get pressure on senior quarterback Avery Johnson, who exited midway through the third quarter of last weekend’s blowout win, the Cougars’ defense could give their team a chance to walk out with a win. WSU saw a quarterback of the same mold in the Apple Cup in Demond Williams Jr., who is a tad more accurate of a thrower than Johnson. Could that be good news for the Cougs and their defense?

That unit will also have to slow down K-State running backs Joe Jackson, Jay Harris and Rodney Fields Jr., the latter of whom earned a surprise start over the veteran Jackson last weekend. Against Nicholls, that trio combined for 192 rushing yards and three scores.

“I think just stopping the run would be the biggest thing, which I think we’ve found that we can do a good job at. They do a lot more gap schemes than UW did,” WSU linebacker Keith Brown said. “They do a lot of pullers, counters, pin-pull, stuff like that. So just being physical at the point of attack and then stopping the run, because they have three really good running backs, kinda like a three-headed horse back there. So if we can stop that, then I think we’ll be in a good spot.”

Washington State.title: I appreciate the chance to cover every WSU game. This Saturday's is a little extra special | Commentary
Washington State.summary:
There’s a scar on my arm that tells my story so poetically that Stephen King might blush. It’s on the underside of my left arm, a few inches below my wrist, a white mark about an inch across. It’s mostly imperceptible if you aren’t looking for it, but if you are, you notice it right away.

Which is the perfect way to capture my journey, to paint the picture of the grind it took for me to earn the chance to come home and cover this weekend’s game between Washington State and Kansas State. On Saturday morning, I’ll wake up in my hometown of Manhattan, Kansas. I’ll head to Bill Snyder Family Stadium, the site of the game, the same venue I grew up attending games at. And I’ll cover the Cougars for The Spokesman-Review, the job that affords me the opportunity in the first place.

This means more than I can put into words, which is saying something for a guy whose whole job is to put things into words. I got my start in this business covering K-State sports for my hometown newspaper, the Manhattan Mercury, which means I have covered dozens of football games at Bill Snyder Family Stadium. It’ll be my first time covering a game there since the fall of 2019, the semester before I graduated.

But to return here, I had to earn my scars, which I mean literally. Here’s what happened: In the spring of 2022, I was at my second job, which was covering Idaho State and high school sports for a newspaper called the Idaho State Journal. I was covering a state tournament game in the Boise area, and because I was covering the last game of the night at this ballpark, the athletic director I was sharing the press box with said he was leaving – just make sure I locked the door on my way out. Sure, no problem, I said.

So when I filed my story and sent out the next day’s sports section of the newspaper, I packed up all my things, walked out of the press box and headed for the exit. One problem: The front gate, a tall metal arrangement, was locked. I strolled around to a side area, where there was a shorter chain-link fence. I didn’t know anyone in this area – I was based about three hours away – so I couldn’t call anyone and ask them to unlock the gate for me.

That left me with two choices: try to scale the front gate, which was much taller with a concrete sidewalk landing. Or climb over the chain-link fence, which was much shorter with a grass landing. Climbing over the chain-link fence looked dangerous in its own right, with sharp spokes poking out, but I figured I could avoid those on my way over – and besides, landing on grass sounded way safer.

So that’s the route I chose. I lightly tossed my backpack over the fence, then hauled myself over. Everything seemed to be going smoothly. But after I lifted myself over, on my way down I got caught on one of the fence’s spokes, gashing my arm. When I checked it out, the cut was fairly deep. Blood was flowing out.

Thankfully, the rest of the story unfolded relatively uneventfully – after wrapping the cut up, I went to get a tetanus shot at Walgreen’s the next morning because I was a bit past due – but it’s the meaning that makes this experience so special for me. To me, my scar mirrors my journey perfectly: In my fourth season working the type of job I wanted for years, covering power conference sports for a major newspaper, I don’t think about it much. Nobody notices the cut nor the journey behind it, and I don’t expect them to.

But when you look for it, you notice it easily. You realize there’s more to the story, just as there’s more to mine. I like to think I have earned every bit of the opportunity to cover Saturday’s game, which is what makes this experience so deeply meaningful to me. I began my professional career covering high schools for the Post Register, which made me a better reporter than I understood at the time. I then spent a little more than a year working at the Idaho State Journal, which is when this injury happened. I have always prided myself on my work ethic and my writing chops, the skills I used to stay grounded and keep building.

But in my story, everything leads back to Manhattan, which I like to call a jumbo-sized Pullman. This place, and by extension K-State, made me. I’m a product of all the people who poured into me growing up: Jordan Jellison, who gave me my first gig at the Mercury; Kristy Nyp, my journalism teacher at Manhattan High; Steve Smethers and Bonnie Bressers, two of my most formative journalism professors at K-State; plus the gang of guys I worked with at the Mercury who I consider some of my best friends: Ryan Black, Justin Toscano, Sean Collins and Shane Thurston, who taught me more than they might ever know.

I’ll never forget the grueling hours I spent covering the Wildcats in college. The 13-hour days that sent me from morning high school cross country meets to K-State football games to Wildcat volleyball matches, the creative stories on K-State nutrition staffers that only a part-time writer like myself had the time for, the chance to travel with Ryan and Justin to road games around the area. I sacrificed lots of weekends and nights, as I always have, but I was having a blast.

Growing up, I remember going to K-State’s game against UCF in 2010, when a foreboding storm cloud moved over the stadium and terrified 12-year-old me. I remember watching the Wildcats rise to the No. 1 spot in the BCS standings in 2012, fueled by quarterback-turned-coach Collin Klein, only for them to suffer a crushing loss to Baylor, which I watched in my childhood home basement with one of my closer friends to this day. And I vividly remember sitting on press row in 2019, when Cartier Diarra threw down a windmill dunk to bury rival Kansas and send a packed Bramlage Coliseum into a deafening frenzy.

Having a front-row seat to moments like those made the beginning of my career, when I was covering high schools and living in a dirt-cheap basement apartment in Idaho Falls, feel like a shock. Depressing. One Saturday afternoon, I sat on that navy leather couch and just sobbed, feeling like I was so far away from my dreams: How did I end up here? How did I end up in a random town in Idaho, covering high schools nobody had ever heard of, living in a basement during the height of the pandemic?

I felt grateful to land a journalism job in such a crazy time in the world, and I spent my first couple months in Idaho Falls energized and excited to tackle my first full-time job. But when the weather turned a bit cooler and I saw the rest of the so-called big-time sports world move on without me, some of my friends landing at the kinds of Power Five and pro beat jobs I once envisioned getting soon after graduating, I felt discouraged.

I don’t mean to make those days sound miserable, because for the most part, I look back at them fondly. I got to meet some incredible people and enjoyed some awesome experiences. I drank cheap beer at a Pocatello bar called Hooligan’s with some friends, which was mostly the same group that I played Monday night basketball with before heading across the street to Applebee’s for drinks (I always got strawberry lemonade, much to the guys’ chagrin). They say the people make the place, and the friends and coaches and players and administrators I met in those years helped make the long grind enjoyable.

In my career, I’ve placed a high priority on not making things about me. It’s about the readers, the audience, the people you cover and the relationships you build. That’s why I rarely write columns and, even in the more creative stories I’ve tackled, I have been loath to use the first person. I’ve worked carefully to hone my voice in my writing, but generally speaking, nobody is reading your stuff for you. They’re reading because they care about the people and the programs you cover. And besides, my career path is far from unique.

With this column, I’m making an exception. I am so beyond grateful for the journey that has led me here. I would never have drawn it up for myself ahead of time, but when I look back, I feel much more fulfilled. I now have the most loving girlfriend and the sweetest dog, the friendliest roommates and the most rewarding job. Life is good.

At the beginning of my career, I couldn’t make sense of why I had to start the way I did, just like I found it crazy that I had to jump over a fence just to leave a damn baseball game. But after that injury happened, I texted my friend Justin, who was covering the Atlanta Braves at the time. “Someday you won’t have to deal with that,” he wrote.

Turns out, he was onto something. I’m glad he was, but mostly, I appreciate the grind it took to prove him right.

Greg Woods can be reached at 509-459-5587 or at gregw@spokesman.com.

Washington State.title: Getting to know WSU's next opponent, Kansas State | Q&A with beat writer Ryan Gilbert
Washington State.summary:
To preview Washington State’s next game, a road test against Big 12 foe Kansas State, The Spokesman-Review conferred with K-State beat writer Ryan Gilbert, who covers the Wildcats for GoPowercat.

Here is our Q&A.

1. How did K-State’s offensive line look against Nicholls, and do the injuries to John Pastore and George Fitzpatrick look to hamper the Cats as much as it might seem?

The offensive line checked all the boxes it could on Saturday. There were a lot of questions surrounding this group entering the season, but game No. 1 was a success. That being said, Nicholls is just not a good football team, so it’s tough to get too excited over that performance in the trenches. K-State simply had the bigger, more physically dominant dudes at the point of contact. Anything other than a promising night would have been a concern for the offensive line.

George Fitzpatrick not being able to give it a go didn’t help matters, but Collin Klein & Co. certainly couldn’t have been caught off guard when they learned he had to be sidelined this season. His health condition from last offseason just lingered and lingered, so it’s not like this just happened out of nowhere. There was ample time to create a backup plan. John Pastore, though, was supposed to be not just a starter but a true star at left tackle. His injury, which will sideline him for the season, happened about a month before the season, and then Tanner Morley also had to miss some time late in camp, so everything kind of just compounded at once.

But the short answer here is that Pastore’s injury is a big blow to the offensive line. Not having him in 2026 will sting. And there have been a lot of moving pieces in the last 30 days due to all the injuries. Offensive lines have to jell together, and, well, it’s hard to jell in just a matter of days.

If there’s one thing I took away from Washington State after catching parts of Sunday’s game against Washington, it’s that the Cougars defensive front can really give their team a chance to win this game. If K-State has just an average offensive line this game (or this season), that’d be a success given the circumstances.

2. Who are the main playmakers in K-State’s defense?

Ahead of the season, the easy answer would have been Oklahoma State transfer Wendell Gregory. But against Nicholls, the junior defensive end really didn’t do much. Of course, it’s way too early to write him off, but many expected him to absolutely feast in 2026, and to not move the needle against an FCS program isn’t exactly promising.

While Gregory had a quiet game, Darien Whitaker stepped up with a strip sack. It seems like his stock is really rising. While he’s listed as a linebacker, expect to see him line up at the edge on defense.

A couple of guys had great games against Nicholls, though – linebacker Gabe Powers and safety Logan Bartley. Powers, who previously spent time at Ohio State, was listed as a starter on the depth chart ahead of the first game, but nobody expected him to have the impact he did. He was great. Meanwhile, Bartley was much the same story – just a solid piece who had some big hits in the secondary.

It’s also worth noting that linebacker Mekhi Mason’s status for Saturday is up in the air due to injury. He’ll be worth monitoring as the teams go through warmups, as he’s a prominent piece on defense.

3. How could Cougar fans expect the Cats to use their tight ends, which has been a strength of the program for quite a while?

As a former five-star, there shouldn’t need to be any endorsement given to tight end Linkon Cure. His upside is clearly there. However, we just haven’t seen him impact the game in a purple jersey. His freshman year in 2025 was very underwhelming, and Saturday against Nicholls was bland. The only direction for him to go is up, but he’s got plenty of meat left on the bone. He’s a player to definitely keep a sharp eye on, but to say he’s a true difference-maker right now would be a bit rich.

Fellow tight end Garrett Oakley has been in the program for as long as QB Avery Johnson has, so these two obviously have a great connection. Many deem him to be one of the top tight ends in the Big 12. Last season, Oakley dropped countless routine passes, so as long as he can simply hang on to the football, Oakley is definitely a red zone threat for the offense.

4. How much can you take away from such a lopsided win over an FCS team?

There are certain areas worth investing more into than others. For example, as we talked about, the offensive line looked good simply because of how bad Nicholls was.

On the flip side, though, K-State’s effort, focus, execution and buy-in were at a top-notch level. The Cats committed only one penalty on Saturday – that has nothing to do with Nicholls.

Overall, take it all with a grain of salt, but you can’t fault a group for simply beating the team that lied on its schedule.

5. What are the main strengths of RBs Rodney Fields and Joe Jackson, and is there any way WSU could slow them down?

It was pretty surprising to see Rodney Fields get the start at the running back spot, as pretty much everyone assumed Joe Jackson would technically be RB1. But that speaks more to how good Fields was in camp than anything. Fields and Jackson are very quality backs.

Just take a look at what Jackson did against Utah last season. He can absolutely be your workhorse.

Fields, on the other hand, has great speed and vision.

Lastly, Jay Harris is definitely in the doghouse after a fumble against Nicholls, so we’ll see how much he plays, but he certainly is worth mentioning. He is, in fact, the clear RB3, but he’s a lot closer to being the third head of a three-headed monster than he is to riding the bench for the entire game.

Washington State.title: WSU faces tough test on the road, UW should cruise at home | Picks of the week
Washington State.summary:
Arizona State coach Kenny Dillingham has proven himself an expert in developing quarterbacks during his three seasons in Tempe. His program also has performed exceedingly well as a road underdog. Those matters are linked, of course, and the latest test of their interconnectivity comes Saturday.

The Sun Devils are 14.5-point underdogs at Texas A&M. How quarterback Cutter Boley performs will determine whether they are within striking range of the 10th-ranked Aggies in the fourth quarter — and, by extension, whether the Big 12 is positioned to collect what would be a first-class victory.

To this point, Dillingham has excelled in comparable situations: He’s 4-1 against the spread as a double-digit underdog away from home since taking charge of his alma mater.

The Sun Devils covered the spread as double-digit underdogs at Cal, Washington and UCLA in 2023 – they beat the Bruins straight up, in fact – and against Texas in the epic 2024 College Football Playoff quarterfinal. The lone failure to cover was at Utah three years ago.

Boley has started one game for the Sun Devils, the 70-7 home victory over Morgan State last weekend that will have zero relevance Saturday morning. In College Station, he will face a talented, well-coached defense and the din generated by 102,000 fans.

But Boley has experience with SEC crowds from his two-year tenure at Kentucky. The key numbers aren’t stellar: He threw five touchdowns and nine interceptions in road games against South Carolina, Georgia, Auburn, Vanderbilt, Florida and Texas.

Which brings us to the Dillingham-as-QB-whisperer component.

Can he conjure a crisp, efficient performance from Boley that looks nothing like the junior’s previous showings in SEC stadiums?

If so, the Sun Devils will be positioned to record a major upset that would both elevate their profile and do wonders for the Big 12, which desperately needs a breakthrough victory in one of several Week 2 matchups against SEC and Big Ten opponents.

Non-conference success, especially against the two leagues that dominate the sport, could lead to the Big 12 placing an at-large team in the College Football Playoff.

Someone needs to step forward. Given Dillingham’s knack for upside surprises, Arizona State is an option worth monitoring.

To the Week 2 picks …

(All times Pacific)

Washington State (+18.5) at Kansas State

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on TNT

Comment: The logistics are daunting for WSU, which played a taxing game Sunday in Seattle and is traveling halfway across the country — on a short week, no less — to play an early (body clock) game in the heat against a host that cruised to victory last weekend. Pick: Kansas State

Oregon (-18.5) at Oklahoma State

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ESPN

Comment: The Ducks didn’t look like a team that can win the national championship in their narrow victory over Boise State, but the Cowboys didn’t look like a team that can win any games in their loss to Tulsa. We’ve seen this script from the Ducks before. Dan Lanning will have them ready to roll. Pick: Oregon

Oklahoma (+2.5) at Michigan

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on Fox

Comment: It was bad enough that Michigan needed a controversial extra second to beat Western Michigan. But quarterback Bryce Underwood isn’t responding well to the criticism, including a warning from coach Kyle Whittingham that his play must improve. Meanwhile, the Sooners are loaded on defense. Pick: Oklahoma

Arizona State (+14.5) at Texas A&M

Kickoff: 9 a.m. on ABC

Comment: The Texas heat won’t be a problem for the Sun Devils, but the Kyle Field crowd could cause communication problems early. We expect a slow start and strong finish from the visitors. And for the game to be in doubt with five minutes remaining. Pick: Arizona State

Utah State (+26.5) at Washington

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: If the Huskies play the way they did in the Apple Cup, they will win by 20. If they play better than they did in the Apple Cup, they will win by 40. Or didn’t you notice that Utah State lost at home to Idaho State by double digits? Yikes. Pick: Washington

Arizona (+7.5) at BYU

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on Fox

Comment: This has the potential to be one of the best games of the day, anywhere. After all, the teams went to double overtime in Tucson 11 months ago, and the competitive balance hasn’t changed significantly. The Cougars pose a supreme test of Arizona’s defensive front, which couldn’t stop BYU’s ground game (258 yards) last year. The winner jumps to the head of the line in the Big 12 title race. Pick: BYU

Cal (+3.5) at Syracuse

Kickoff: 12:30 p.m. on ACC Network

Comment: A demoralizing loss in the opener, followed by a long trip to face a low-profile opponent that generates zero urgency? Feels like a trap game for the Bears, even though winless teams with new coaches should not be in position to get trapped. Pick: Syracuse

Memphis (+8.5) at Boise State

Kickoff: 3 p.m. on USA Network

Comment: No game in Week 2 carries greater playoff implications, not even the Texas-Ohio State showdown. After all, there is only one playoff berth reserved for the best team in the Group of Five, and the winner in Boise instantly becomes the favorite. The Broncos looked like a CFP team last weekend at Oregon. They need a comparable performance Saturday. Pick: Memphis

San Diego State (+12.5) at UCLA

Kickoff: 4:15 p.m. on Big Ten Network

Comment: The Bruins are soaring with confidence after opening the Bob Chesney era with a convincing victory at Cal. Do the Aztecs have enough on the lines of scrimmage to stand tall for 60 minutes? Is SDSU quarterback Jayden Denegal capable of an error-free game against a Big Ten defense? We aren’t convinced on either front. Pick: UCLA

Ohio State (+1.5) at Texas

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on ABC

Comment: The best non-conference duel of the season is a rematch of Ohio State’s 14-7 victory last year. That was the season opener for both teams, and Texas quarterback Arch Manning looked rattled throughout. He should be sharper this time against a reloading Buckeyes defense. Enjoy it, folks. If the playoff expands to 24 teams next year, these blue-blood showdowns will have far lower stakes. Pick: Texas

Texas Tech (+26.5) at Oregon State

Kickoff: 4:30 p.m. on CBS

Comment: The Beavers were grittier than expected in their opener under new coach JaMarcus Shepard, a 13-point loss at Houston. Meanwhile, Texas Tech was slightly less than overwhelming against Abilene Christian. If OSU quarterback Braden Atkinson avoids major mistakes, the Red Raiders could have trouble clearing the high bar set by the oddsmakers. Pick: Oregon State

Arkansas (+12.5) at Utah

Kickoff: 7:15 p.m. on ESPN

Comment: One of the few Big 12 vs. SEC matchups this season should not be competitive in the fourth quarter: The Utes have too many playmakers for Arkansas, which is rebuilding under coach Ryan Silverfield and lacks the high-end talent present on so many SEC rosters. If the Utes win, they should be undefeated entering the back half of the schedule in late October. Pick: Utah

Straight-up winners: Oregon, Oklahoma, Texas A&M, Kansas State, Washington, BYU, Syracuse, Boise State, UCLA, Texas, Texas Tech and Utah

Five-star special: Kansas State. We commend Washington State for agreeing to play the Apple Cup on a Sunday. But goodness, they are facing some serious logistical challenges with the short turnaround and lengthy trip.

Washington State.title: 'I started sobbing': Behind WSU LB Keith Brown's return to action after missing last season to injury
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – The moment began to wash over Keith Brown some 10 minutes before kickoff, the gravity hitting him like a tsunami. He sat in his locker inside Husky Stadium, waiting to take the field for Sunday’s Apple Cup, the nervous energy of tens of thousands of fans pounding outside the steel walls. He had waited six years for his moment, a chance to start a season opener, an opportunity to demonstrate his arrival at Washington State.

For a moment, the senior linebacker looked up and glanced to his left, where he saw veteran wide receiver Darrius Clemons with a bit of moisture around his eyes.

That’s when it hit Brown.

“I started sobbing,” Brown said.

Right before the biggest moment of his college career, the first game of his sixth and final season, Brown felt everything crash over him at once: the two years at Oregon, the redshirt year at Louisville, the first year at WSU and then the second, which he missed due to a shoulder injury. He had started a handful of games as a freshman five years ago, but never a season opener, a signal that he had never been the guy.

Now he is. He’s one of WSU’s two starting linebackers. On Sunday, he was entrusted with some of the game’s biggest moments, like the Cougars’ goal-line stop right before halftime. He led the team with six tackles, all solo, illustrating the level of playmaking that made him the top-rated prospect in all of Oregon during high school.

“Missing last year was really hard for me,” Brown said. “And then, I’ve waited my turn six years to start Week 1, so yeah, it was a really emotional moment for me. It felt good to be out there again, it really did.”

Brown certainly played like it. Right before halftime, the Huskies had fourth-and-goal from the Cougars’ 1-yard line, threatening to go up three scores. Things were tilting for WSU, whose offense was slogging and scuffling through a slow start to the game. Go down three scores here and the visitors’ path to a comeback would become just about impossible.

So Brown leapt into action. UW quarterback Demond Williams Jr. took a shotgun snap and handed it off to running back Jayden Limar, who plunged up the middle. He was met in the gap by a host of Cougar defenders. In the middle was Brown, who wrapped Limar up around the midsection and drove him backward. A sea of WSU defenders surged into the pile, forcing officials to blow the play dead before Limar could generate any more forward momentum.

Thinking back on the play now, Brown remembers his assignment: He was to look at center Kolt Dietrich and make his move accordingly. If Dietrich went left, Brown would pursue off his right hip, and vice versa. He figured he would have to wade through a mass of bodies if he wanted to make the stop.

“And when I was running through the gap, a guy showed up in front of me,” Brown laughed. “I didn’t realize it was Jirah who threw him around.”

Turns out, Brown realized after the fact, that WSU defensive tackle Jirah Leaupepetele hadn’t just won his rep against UW left guard John Mills, a consensus freshman All-American last season. He had thrown him to the left, paving the way for Brown to meet Limar in the gap. Several Cougar defenders converged to create a pile-up and push Limar back, but the stop began with Leaupepetele and his physicality up front.

“Kudos to Jirah for being as grown as he is,” Brown said.

Across the next 90 minutes or so, Brown and the Cougars’ defense continued to make things hard on the Huskies, who needed two fourth-quarter touchdowns – and one critical third-down conversion with about two minutes to play – to finally put away Kirby Moore’s team for good. But all things considered, Brown says he feels good about what he and his unit put on display in Seattle, giving their team a chance to draw within one in the fourth quarter on two different occasions.

This week, as Washington State prepares for a road test against Big 12 foe Kansas State, Brown says the emotions he felt before Sunday’s game haven’t followed him around. He’s trying to stay in the moment, he says, keeping blinders on ahead of another critical Power Four game. As one of the leaders of this defense, Brown finds it important to stay even-keeled and focused.

Part of that, he says, has required changing his approach to the season. Toward the end of the Cougars’ fall camp, Brown and the WSU defense had been flourishing, becoming the story of camp. “We were feeling on top of the world,” Brown said. Then one day, that unit turned in a forgettable practice, and defensive coordinator Trent Bray let them hear about it. He encouraged his players to delete all social media apps off their phones, including Instagram and Twitter, so that they wouldn’t see posts about themselves and get too high or low.

As he thought about it, Brown realized he agreed. He would rather not see articles about him and his team, positive or negative. Sometimes they still find their way to his phone thanks to his mom, Sarah – “I’m like, ‘Mom, I don’t want to see them,’ ” Brown said with a smile – but the decision is still helping Brown block out the outside noise.

“I could easily think that I’m this or I’m that,” Brown said. “But realistically, I have to get better every week. If you even look back on it, I still didn’t play my best game, not even close. I left some on the table. There’s reads I could have filled faster and stuff like that, but yeah, every week just wanna get better.”

“Keith is as consistent as it gets,” WSU defensive end Linus Zunk said. “I mean, I’ve been able to practice alongside him for a long time now, so really out there, it’s just replicating what I already see of him in practice and the way that he communicates and keeps the defense together. So he’s definitely doing a great job in that.”

Mostly, though, Brown just appreciates the opportunity to do so in the first place.

***

A little more than a year later, Brown calls it a “stupid mistake by the two of us.” It was early in fall camp last season, and on a sweltering afternoon at Rogers Practice Field, he got into it with running back Kirby Vorhees. The two argued and things turned physical. In the heat of the moment, Brown got his shoulder tangled up with Vorhees before they were separated by their teammates.

At first, Brown remembers, he didn’t think the injury was serious. Moments after the scuffle, he worked with trainer Brian Oelke to pop his shoulder back into place.

“I was like, all right, doesn’t feel too bad,” Brown said. “I was gonna continue practicing.”

But Oelke advised against it, holding Brown out of the rest of the practice. The next morning, Brown woke and realized things could be serious. “I couldn’t even sit up,” he said. “It was more serious than I thought it was at all.”

So Brown had his shoulder checked out. He went through examinations, an X-ray and an MRI, which showed a labrum tear, which Brown could have played through. Doctors expected that much. What they weren’t prepared for were the results of an MRI, which showed additional bone breakage around the tear, which made the injury serious, risking the stability of the entire shoulder.

So Brown consulted with team medical director and orthopaedic surgeon Ed Tingstad, who told Brown, “You’re an adult. At the end of the day, you can make your own decision.” Brown chatted with former coaches, former teammates. “Everyone was kinda pointing in the direction of, if I were to play last year, I would have to get surgery after the year no matter what, and then I’d miss all of training, pro day and stuff like that. So I was like, OK, let’s just get surgery and try it again.”

Brown admits that at first, he had a hard time accepting that his season would end before it even started, that he wouldn’t get a chance to play in the middle of what turned out to be one of the country’s best defenses. That fall, the Cougars went on to give legitimate scares to Power Four opponents like Ole Miss and Virginia, both one-score contests in the fourth quarter.

Brown always tuned into those. That year, he was teammates with former running back Dylan Paine, who was also out with an injury. They set up a system: During games, they would be in their rooms on a Discord call with each other. On one screen, they had a monitor to play a video game called Arc Raiders. On the other, they would have the broadcast of the WSU game, chatting with each other about the video game and the football game.

Around that time, Brown says, he had gotten over the initial shock of missing the season – “I was like, OK, it is what it is, let’s attack this,” he said of his surgery – but the thought of being able to make an impact in those games, in the Cougars’ close defeats to the likes of Ole Miss and Virginia and James Madison, pulled at him.

“Those are games you want to play in,” he said. “I love playing big games. It’s always something I’ve really enjoyed. It is hard to watch. It is for sure. You always root for your teammates, obviously, but you’re like, dang, I wish I was out there, you know?”

By the spring, he was. He was cleared to return to action ahead of WSU’s spring ball. At first, he says, he felt a bit anxious about putting his shoulder to the test. But he trusted the advice of Tingstad, who reassured Brown that, yes, his shoulder might sting a bit the first few times he made contact with a teammate or a sled. But unless something drastic happens, Tingstad told Brown, he wouldn’t reinjure it. Even better for Brown: He didn’t have any scar tissue, which some athletes get after surgery.

Then came summertime, when Brown felt even more like himself. He became roommates with Vorhees, who he considers one of his closer friends on the team. At around 7 a.m. on Saturday mornings, Brown says, he would often hear Vorhees banging on his desk in frustration. He was playing Fortnite, Brown realized later on.

It’s a moment Brown laughs about in hindsight, like others recently. Neither Brown nor Vorhees took their tussle personally. It was just two competitors letting their tempers flare for a moment, Brown says now, chalking it up to a hot day and a deep sense of wanting to win.

As his final season of college football unfolds, Brown feels that more than ever. He wants to make this season count, wants to squeeze every last drop out of this experience. It’s why he deleted all social media off his phone. It’s why he practices hard and watches game film even harder.

Has the finality of it all hit Brown, who has been playing college football since 2021? Not yet, he says. He’s more focused on taking things week-by-week, and this week, that means honing on K-State and the Wildcats’ offense. Last weekend, he felt the emotions hit him like a Mack truck. Not since.

“It’ll probably hit me again on senior night when my mom and everyone’s out there and stuff like that. It’ll probably hit me again after the bowl game,” Brown said. “I think throughout the weeks and stuff like that, you don’t really think about it. You just prepare and go play.”

Washington State.title: Cougars Fall to Washington in Apple Cup, 24-10
In Apple Cup loss to Washington, Cougars' third-down woes might have more to do with first and second down | WSU rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Have your pick at what could be the biggest problem Washington State faced on offense in Sunday’s Apple Cup loss to Washington.

Could it be the Cougars’ turnover problem? Sure, they lost three. What about their running game? Possibly. They got only 48 combined yards from their running backs . How about their inefficiency in the kicking game? That’s valid too . Kicker Jack Stevens misfired on two field goals, including one that was moved back five yards following a pre-snap penalty.

The one that looms perhaps the largest, though, is that WSU went 0-for-11 on third down. Good luck winning many games with that. In fact, it bothered quarterback Caden Pinnick so much that in a postgame news conference, he cut himself off from an answer on a different topic to say this: “I’m just thinking about the 0-for-11 right now.”

That made things nearly impossible for the Cougars’ offense, even when they climbed back into the game with two scores in the fourth quarter: a rushing touchdown from Pinnick and a field goal from Stevens, both of which pulled the Cougs to within one score.

But here’s the interesting rub about that number: Rough as WSU’s day on third down was, the Cougars put themselves in some tough situations thanks to their first- and second-down plays. That set up several challenging third -down looks, including two third-and-longs and three third-and-shorts. WSU’s average yards-to-go on third down was about 7, which is far from an easy situation, especially in a raucous Husky Stadium.

After the game, WSU coach Kirby Moore seemed to be aware of the problem, possibly without seeing the numbers first: “You gotta go back to first and second down first, and we gotta be more efficient,” Moore said. “We gotta create more explosives there on first and second down. And then third -and -long and XL, they’ve got a really good front, and sometimes that front was getting there a little bit quicker than we wanted it to. So that’s something we gotta look at.”

Here are a few numbers that illustrate the point.

On first down, the Cougars mostly excelled, averaging 7 yards per play. They ran 12 rushes for a total of 70 yards, which is an average rush of 5.8 yards. Pinnick also completed 10 of 12 passes on first down for 107 yards, an average of 10.7 yards per play.

But the Cougars also got behind the chains on a couple occasions. In one scenario, left guard Kyle Martin was called for a false start, underscoring his forgettable first start at the college level. And on another first down, WSU lost 2 yards, resulting in a second-and-12. That’s no way to take down a Husky defense that’s already on track to live up to its billing as one of the country’s best units this fall.

For WSU, the bigger problem came on second down. The Cougars rushed seven times for a total of 17 yards, an average of 2.4 yards. That’s about a 1.5-yard difference from their output on first down, largely explained by their insistence on running up the middle, which often went nowhere. That’s one adjustment WSU offensive coordinator Matt Miller would be wise to make headed into Saturday’s game at Kansas State.

Here are Pinnick’s numbers on second down: 5-for-10 passing for 30 yards and one interception, which came on a dropped pass in the fourth quarter. Pinnick also took one sack on second down, which resulted in a 4-yard loss.

Overall, WSU’s second-down plays went for an average of 2.4 yards.

“We gotta be more efficient and explosive on first and second down, and create more manageable third downs,” Moore said. “Third-and-7-plus against anyone in college football, it’s gonna be difficult. The protection’s gotta hold up. Obviously, routes downfield. The defense usually has an advantage in those situations, so we have to do a better job on first and second down.”

It’s no secret that the Cougs slogged through a bleak third-down effort, and while they could have remedied that problem with better efficiency on first and second down, third downs are a part of the game. For the game, they averaged a shade under 2 yards per play on third down.

They also took two sacks on third down. WSU’s offensive line gave up 13 quarterback pressures, according to Pro Football Focus, four apiece from Martin and right tackle Jonny Lester, plus three from right guard Nick Bakken and two from center Noah Dunham. The Cougars likely won’t play a better defense than the Huskies’ this season, but those numbers must improve for their offense to follow suit.

At the same time, though, the bigger problem in the Cougars’ third-down scenarios actually seems to be the first- and second-down scenarios that precede them. Look for Moore and Miller to make adjustments accordingly before they embark on their second straight Power 4 tilt to open the season.

Washington State.title: WSU heads to the Midwest to take on Kansas State in second-straight Power 4 game to open season | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s road game against Kansas State on Saturday morning.

What is it? In the teams’ first meeting, Washington State heads to the Midwest to take on Big 12 foe Kansas State, which is coming off a lopsided 71-3 win over FCS Nicholls. The home-and-home series, which includes a 2029 matchup in Pullman, was brokered in 2016 by former WSU president Kirk Schulz – who had recently held the same position at K-State.

It’s the second straight road Power 4 game to open the season for the Cougars, who are coming off a loss in Sunday’s Apple Cup to No. 17 Washington.

Where is it? Bill Snyder Family Stadium in Manhattan, Kansas.

When is it? Kickoff is set for 9 a.m. (11 a.m. local time)

Where can I watch it? TNT will broadcast the game, with streaming available on HBO Max.

Who is favored? As of Monday afternoon, WSU was around an 181/2-point underdog in most sportsbooks.

How did the Cougars fare last week? In a 24-10 loss to No. 17 Washington in the first season-opening Apple Cup, WSU’s offense struggled to the tune of three turnovers, two missed field goals and a third-down conversion rate of 0-for-11. The Cougars made things interesting in the fourth quarter – quarterback Caden Pinnick scored on an 11-yard rushing touchdown and kicker Jack Stevens connected on a field goal – but their defense, staunch for the majority of the game, couldn’t produce stops on the ensuing drives.

In WSU coach Kirby Moore’s debut game, the Cougs’ defense shone the most, holding the No. 17 Huskies and quarterback Demond Williams Jr. to just 10 points through three quarters. That included a key goal-line stop right before halftime, when WSU linebacker Keith Brown led the charge in stuffing UW running back Jayden Limar on fourth-and-goal from the 1, sending the visitors into the locker room with a boatload of momentum.

But as was the case for the majority of the game, WSU’s offense couldn’t cash in. In his debut as the Cougars’ new quarterback, the UC Davis transfer Pinnick completed 16 of 25 passes for 142 yards and two interceptions, one of which came on a dropped pass in the fourth quarter. He also registered one rushing touchdown, an 11-yard designed keeper in the fourth quarter, pulling WSU to within 10-7.

“We gotta make sure – and this is overall from an offensive standpoint – our first goal was 100% ball security,” Moore said on Monday. “We did not achieve that, so we gotta do a better job taking care of the football. Had an initial really good start on the first drive. Got in some longer down and distances there on the third downs, which are difficult, and sometimes the defense has a say in the fight, and you gotta be ready to check the ball down, take care of the football. Sometimes it’s OK to punt, and that’s something we gotta really emphasize. Great job responding there in the fourth quarter, and so we gotta build on that.”

In a critical development, the Cougars also lost veteran receiver/kick returner Tony Freeman to an injury. After just 10 snaps, Freeman went down in the first quarter, went to the locker room and returned in street clothes, out for the rest of the game. On Monday, Moore indicated Freeman is likely to miss Saturday’s game with a knee injury, adding that coaches are still waiting on the results of Freeman’s MRI.

On offense, WSU also got impressive games from receivers Daniel Blood (five catches for 57 yards) and Darrius Clemons (three catches for 40 yards). If Freeman misses Saturday’s game, those two will have to step up again for the Cougars, who could also ask more from receivers Tank Hawkins and Branden Ganashamoorthy.

The Cougars’ defense was led by the veteran linebacker Brown, who missed all of last season recovering from a shoulder injury he sustained during fall camp. In Sunday’s game, he looked like he never missed a beat, leading the team with six tackles, all solo.

Scouting Kansas State … K-State opened the season last weekend with a 71-3 romp over FCS Nicholls, which was no match for the Wildcats, who are led by senior quarterback Avery Johnson. In his first game of his final season of college football, he completed 15 of 21 passes for 199 yards and three touchdowns, exiting midway through the third quarter as the Wildcats continued to roll.

K-State has two top running backs: Oklahoma State transfer Rodney Fields, who made a surprise start in Saturday’s game and churned out 14 carries for 101 yards and one score; and veteran returner Joe Jackson, who added seven rushes for 38 yards and one touchdown. All told, seven Wildcats scored touchdowns: Johnson, Fields, Jackson (two), receivers Jaron Tibbs Josh Manning and Brandon White (punt return), plus reserves Jacob Knuth and Monterrio Elston Jr.

It’s the debut season for head coach Collin Klein, who starred as K-State’s quarterback in the early 2010s and went on to become an assistant coach with the Wildcats from 2017-23, then worked as Texas A&M’s offensive coordinator for the 2024 and 2025 seasons before returning to his alma mater as the head coach for this season.

Some names to watch on K-State’s defense include linebacker Gabe Powers and safety Logan Bartley, who tied for a team-leading five tackles against Nicholls, plus Oklahoma State transfer edge rusher Wendell Gregory, who is expected to be one of the Big 12’s best edge rushers this season. In Saturday’s game, the Wildcats piled up 10 tackles for loss, including 1.5 from defensive end Jordan Allen.

“Lot of different sets offensively,” Moore said of Kansas State’s offense. “They do a great job of running the football. The quarterback’s part of it. A lot of different schemes, and then when you get tight, they have a lot of play action concepts that get guys vertically down the field.”

What happened last time?

This is the teams’ first meeting.

Washington State.title: LB Keith Brown leads the way in WSU defense's sterling showing in Apple Cup loss to No. 17 Washington
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – A year ago, Keith Brown watched the Apple Cup in street clothes. He was out of action for last season’s game, as he was for the entire season, sitting out with a shoulder injury he sustained during fall camp.

It was a costly development for the Cougars and their defense, which could have used Brown’s veteran touch at linebacker, in the Apple Cup and beyond. Instead, he had his shoulder in a brace, recovering from the surgery he underwent before the season.

If Brown was itching to get back on the field, he showed it in one play, the best one the Cougars made on defense in a 24-10 loss to No. 17 Washington in Sunday’s Apple Cup: He helped stuff UW tailback Jayden Limar on a fourth-and-goal from the 1 right before halftime, greeting him just before the goal line, a critical stop for that group.

“We practiced it early in the week,” Brown said. “When you have a guy like Jirah (Leaupepetele) and Kaden Beatty in front of you, their job on that is to kinda just open the gap for me. So I was just ready to shoot it when they did. It’s kinda like a timing thing. We practiced it in the week, and it worked out exactly how we practiced.”

Take your pick on what you liked best about the way WSU played on defense in this one. The Cougars turned the Huskies over once on downs. They forced four punts, including two three-and-outs. They permitted just 10 points in the first three quarters, and games may not be won in three quarters, but it’s still an impressive feat for a WSU defensive outfit with lots of new pieces.

For WSU, it registered as a wholly encouraging outing on defense, which kept the team in the game for just about the whole way. The Cougars found themselves within one score in the fourth quarter on two separate occasions, which is far closer than the 24.5-point spread in this game suggested. Much of that credit belongs to WSU defensive coordinator Trent Bray’s unit.

Near the heart of that effort was Brown, who led the team with six total tackles, all of the solo variety. None may have been bigger than his stop at the goal line – a play that required so much individual strength and savvy from the Cougars that it paints a picture of what the unit could flourish into as this season unfolds – but it was his consistency and reliability that stood out most.

That mattered on Sunday, when the Cougars lost three turnovers, one fumble from running back Kirby Vorhees and two interceptions from quarterback Caden Pinnick, one of which came on a dropped pass in the fourth quarter. In those scenarios, Brown and his unit had to jog back onto the field at a moment’s notice, staring at bleak field position. They never looked worse for the wear.

“We just go out there, man. “Our defense is such a unique side of the ball. We don’t really care. I’m not staring at the scoreboard, staring at the minutes, you know? I’m just like, cool. Another opportunity to go out there and do what we’re supposed to do. No series is different than another for me, honestly. We just go out there ready to play.”

Keep this in mind, too: Defensive ends Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk lived up to the billing. They had played so well in spring ball, had generated so much consistent pass rush in fall camp, that they figured to become one of the strengths of the unit. They played like it on Sunday, combining for nine quarterback pressures, five from McLain and four from Zunk.

They bothered UW quarterback Demond Williams Jr. so early in the game that as the rest of the contest unfolded, UW coach Jedd Fisch and the Huskies countered by getting the ball out quicker, running screen plays and quick passes for Williams. It’s a compliment to McLain and Zunk, the pass-rushing duo who figure to treat the Cougars’ future opponents similarly.

In fact, if there’s anything for WSU coach Kirby Moore and assistants to feel encouraged by from Sunday’s game, it’s their defense. They made a couple costly mistakes – missing a tackle on Williams and letting him convert a key third-and-long late in the fourth quarter will sting – but that’s to be expected against a team of the Huskies’ caliber.

The Cougars won’t get much of a reprieve next week, when WSU travels to take on Big 12 foe Kansas State. If Brown and the Cougs’ defense can engineer a defensive outing similar to the one they delivered here on Sunday, they could pry open the door to an upset.

“We already talked about it in the locker room,” Brown said. “We have 11 more opportunities, 11 more guaranteed opportunities to play. So let’s go out there and get better every single week. Let’s attack practice this week even harder. Work on the things that we didn’t do well and just continue to build off that.”

Washington State.title: WSU won’t face a defense like Washington’s again this season. But the Cougars have real concerns on offense | Analysis
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – Somewhere deep within Husky Stadium, the site of Washington State’s 24-10 loss to Washington in Sunday’s Apple Cup, Caden Pinnick began to trail off. In front of a crimson backdrop, he was talking about his outing in the game, the touchdown and two interceptions he registered in his debut as the Cougars’ new quarterback, when he cut himself off.

He shook his head ever so slightly and said, “I’m just thinking about the 0-for-11 right now.”

That would be WSU’s conversion rate on third down for the entire game, a key reason why the Cougars couldn’t generate enough offense to take advantage of their defense’s heroics and climb back into this one. In their first eight drives, they lost two turnovers, totaled just north of 100 total yards of offense and, perhaps most importantly, did not convert a single third down.

That trend hovered over the Cougars’ entire outing on offense, derailing their best-laid plans. They did convert one fourth down, which led to Pinnick’s rushing touchdown in the fourth frame, but WSU will not feel good about this offensive showing. The Cougars lost three total turnovers, missed two field goals, tallied just 38 rushing yards from running backs, submitted two three-and-outs.

Before we get into the weeds on this WSU outing, the first for new head coach Kirby Moore, let’s explore a bit of context. First, it’s likely that for the rest of this season, the Cougars will not face a defense as good as the Huskies’. Washington’s defense, which returns 11 players who made starts from a 2025 outfit that finished No. 11 in total defense, projects to be one of the nation’s finest this fall. For that reason, many of the problems the Cougars faced here on Sunday – inside runs going nowhere, too much pressure on Pinnick, coverage sacks – may not be as prevalent in future games.

Plus, in the second quarter, WSU lost a key receiver to injury: veteran Tony Freeman. It’s unclear what exactly his injury was, but after the game, Moore called it “very unfortunate.” Freeman will get an MRI soon to diagnose the injury and provide a prognosis, Moore added. Freeman is expected to be one of the Cougars’ top receivers this season, if not their absolute best, so that kind of development surely threw a wrench into offensive coordinator Matt Miller’s blueprint and forced him to make adjustments that were never part of it.

Still, for WSU, that injury fits in with the other side of this: Lots of the things the Cougars put on display in this Apple Cup don’t figure to vanish as easily. Plenty of the other problems WSU faced will require fixing, not just putting Washington in the rearview mirror.

Some of the main ones center around playcalling. Perhaps the biggest error Miller and the Cougs made in that department came in the second quarter. Facing a critical third-and-5 near midfield, needing points on this drive to prevent things from getting away from them, the Cougars decided on a shotgun inside handoff for running back Kirby Vorhees. He gained one yard, and punter Max Dean sent it away one play later.

“There’s certain analytics,” Moore said about that play call. “Obviously, you get to a certain down and distance and you wanna be able to go for it on fourth down. We did not. We got 1 (yard). Was expecting hopefully to get a couple more there in that situation.”

On several other occasions, WSU showed a similarly vanilla approach to offense, trying to move bodies on the interior and run up the gut. Here are the yards the Cougars gained on runs up the middle by running backs: 6, minus 1, 3, 4 (fumble from Vorhees), 6, 1, 1, 0, 0, 8. That adds up to 10 carries for 28 yards, an average of 2.8 yards per try. It was clear from near the beginning of the game that the Cougars would not have much luck with that approach.

But throughout the game, Miller and WSU coaches kept at it, which registered as strange. The Cougars surely would like to be able to move linemen up front and run up the gut. But when you’re facing meaningful size and skill disadvantages in that department, it’s time to notice that and adjust accordingly, which didn’t always happen. It puts Miller at risk of making the same mistake that hampered Washington State’s offense for the first half of last season: miscasting players and, for lack of a better phrase, trying to force a round peg in a square hole.

The good news for Miller and the Cougars is that in the playcalling department, he wasn’t always so hard-headed. WSU unlocked some of its best offense when Pinnick rolled out of the pocket, when coaches schemed up space for him to take a second and scan the field, when they got their fastest players – Woods, Tank Hawkins – going to the outsides. They also got two sharp outings from receivers Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons, who combined for eight catches for 97 yards.

With those kinds of moves, Miller showed a deft hand and a keen sense of adjustments, which will be critical for the Cougs this fall.

“Those plays are definitely an in-game feeling. I think we got the ball rolling when we did that,” Pinnick said. “But I have no doubt that coach Miller is gonna put me in the best situation and seemed to be in the best situation to convert on some of these plays. We just gotta get better at some of these situational football plays, and we’ll be better.”

For WSU, the critical part will be this: In future games, in the two Power 4 tilts the Cougars have lined up in the next three weeks, can Miller be as quick to make adjustments? Or will he show the same type of conventional playcalling ideas, the standard dropbacks that resulted in Pinnick taking three sacks and scrambling countless other times from pressure?

“You gotta go back to first and second down first, and we gotta be more efficient,” Moore said. “We gotta create more explosives there on first and second down. And then third and long and XL, they’ve got a really good front, and sometimes that front was getting there a little bit quicker than we wanted it to. So that’s something we gotta look at.”

In Sunday’s game, WSU left guard Kyle Martin registered a Pro Football Focus overall offensive grade of 29.9, which is about 30 points below average. His run-blocking grade was 38.8, lowest on the team, and his pass-blocking grade was an unsightly 5.8, allowing one sack on four total pressures. He slogged through a forgettable game in his first career start at the college level.

But like several other patterns in Sunday’s game, across the rest of this season, Martin and WSU won’t face the same kinds of problems that the Huskies presented. The one key question: Can the Cougars make enough adjustments to avoid finding themselves in those types of situations to begin with? The answer may play an outsize role in how the rest of Moore’s debut season unfolds.

Cougar Men to Face Seattle U at Seattle Holiday Classic in December
WSU hoops to meet Seattle U at Seattle Holiday Classic in December
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Chalk up another game on Washington State’s nonconference hoops schedule.

The Cougars will meet Seattle University on Dec. 19 at the Seattle Holiday Classic, according to a Monday news release, set for Climate Pledge Arena. It’s part of a doubleheader showcase, which will also pit University of Washington against Baylor.

“We’re looking forward to getting back to Seattle and bringing Cougar basketball to the thousands of WSU alumni in western Washington,” WSU coach David Riley said in the release. “I believe playing the other Division-I teams in the state is an important part of developing the game and honoring its history in the Pacific Northwest. We look forward to facing the Redhawks at Climate Pledge Arena and welcoming Coug fans to the Seattle Holiday Classic.”

It’ll be the third meeting in the last two seasons for WSU and Seattle U, which split last season’s series, then a West Coast Conference matchup. The Redhawks earned a 69-55 win in Seattle, and the Cougars followed with a 70-58 victory about a month later in Pullman.

It also represents another chance for each head coach to match wits. Riley and Seattle U coach Chris Victor were both assistant coaches at Eastern Washington from 2015-17. In fact, both head coaches ran the same first play during their first matchup last season in Seattle.

“The same exact first set, a Spain action,” Riley said after that game. “Just totally random. I thought it was funny. We worked together for a couple years at Eastern. He’s a great person. Every once in awhile, you can have some fun in these games.”

WSU’s next roster includes 13 newcomers: Mohamed Sankhe (France), East Texas A&M transfer forward Ronnie Harrison, Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (DII) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Sancho Moraga (Spain), Roman Stathis (Australia), Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele, Eastern Washington transfer wing Casey Jones (who was previously on a two-year church mission), Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and freshman forward Brayden Kyman.

Here is WSU’s known nonconference slate.

• At Washington (exh.), TBA.

• Vs. Davidson, TBA.

• Vs. Duke (Palm Springs), Nov. 21.

• Vs. Idaho, Nov. 27.

• At Murray State, Nov. 30.

• Vs. North Dakota State, Dec. 6.

• At Seattle U, Dec. 19

• Vs. EWU (Spokane), Dec. 22.

• At LSU, Dec. 28.

Washington State.title: WSU lands commitment from French big man Mohamed Sankhe, rounding out next roster
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Washington State has landed the final piece of its next men’s basketball roster.

The Cougars have officially landed French big man Mohamed Sankhe, he announced on social media on Thursday, becoming the final player on coach David Riley’s 2026-27 team. Listed at 6-foot-10, Sankhe is the mysterious post player Riley had been alluding to in news conferences since the spring.

Born in Senegal, Sankhe most recently played for Jean D’Arc Vichy Clermont Metropole in French Pro B, the second-tier pro hoops league in France. Across 41 games in the last international season, Sankhe averaged 5.3 points, 5.5 rebounds in 18 minutes per game, shooting an efficient 54% from the field.

More recently in this summer’s U20 Euro Championships, Sankhe averaged 10 points and 6.8 rebounds per game, turning in a similarly efficient field goal percentage of 56%, leading France to the semifinals. He scored in double-digits twice, including a double-double against Croatia (18 points, 11 rebounds) and an 11-point outing against Germany, including nine rebounds that game. He did not record any blocked shots in that span.

It’s unclear what kind of role Sankhe will play this upcoming season, but at the very least, he gives the Cougars some needed size. WSU has two traditional big men on the roster, including 6-foot-8 UNLV transfer Ladji Dembele and 6-foot-10 returner Dominik Robinson. They also have 6-foot-9 Northwestern transfer Tyler Kropp, but he’s expected to play the small forward or power forward spots for Riley’s team.

What the Cougs might have been lacking is a true big man, which came back to bite last season’s team, which often struggled to contain opposing big men with real size. That could be where they enjoy the presence of Sankhi, who collected four games with double-digit rebounds last international season, including one with 13 boards and another with 12. He figures to have little trouble hitting the glass for WSU.

Sankhe appears to be a true post player. Last international season, which included 41 games from September 2025 to this April, he did not attempt a single 3-pointer. In that way, he doesn’t fit the mold of a traditional Riley stretch big, but WSU does have a player like that in Dembele, who has shot 33% on 1.1 attempts from deep in his 70-game college career.

Can Sankhe be a true rim protector? That much is unclear. Last international season, Sankhe averaged just 0.4 blocks per game. That’s the kind of number you might expect from a guard, not a 6-foot-10 center. To his credit, he did record three games with two blocks, and he was playing fewer than 20 minutes per game. But Sankhe might have to become a more imposing rim defender for the Cougars to flourish on defense in his minutes.

Sankhe makes three international player’s on this WSU team, including Spanish freshman guard Pedro Sancha Moraga and Australia native Roman Stathis. Sankhe is also the 13th newcomer on the Cougars’ roster, joining a bevy of transfers from around the country that Riley used to restock a depleted roster from the offseason.

Those include East Texas A&M transfer forward Ronnie Harrison, Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (DII) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Moraga, Stathis, Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, Dembele, Eastern Washington transfer wing Casey Jones (who was previously on a two-year church mission), Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and freshman forward Brayden Kyman.
